source_span: Because the architecture of retinal vessels is predominantly planar ( Paques et al . , 2003 ) , we believe that our technique is well suited to study the complete retinal network , with a potentially lower measurement error .
keep_reasoning: Connects anatomy to the study's methodological suitability, a point likely to appear in a lay summary explaining why the retina is an advantageous target.

fact: A limitation of the study is the requirement to sequentially track blood flow in each vessel rather than measuring all vessels at once.
source_span: A limitation of our study is the requirement to sequentially track flow in each vessel .
keep_reasoning: Describes a practical limitation readers would want to know about when assessing the method's throughput and applicability.

fact: The system's 5° field of view allows simultaneous tracking of up to two first-generation vessels or up to five capillaries, but the authors tracked vessels one-by-one to maximize pixel density and measurement signal-to-noise ratio.
source_span: While the maximum field of view of our system of 5° enables tracking flow in up to two first-generation vessels simultaneously , and up to five capillaries on the other end of the size spectrum , we tracked flow on a vessel by vessel basis in this study to maximize the pixel density and measurement SNR on each vessel .
keep_reasoning: Explains current practical limits on simultaneous measurements and why the team chose sequential tracking to improve data quality.

fact: The technique currently cannot measure velocity in all first-generation vessels around the optic disk because it requires an optimal (~5–45°) angle between the vessel and the 1D scanning beam.
source_span: A remaining challenge of our study is the current inability to track velocity in all first-generation vessels around the optic disk , because of the requirement of an optimal ( ~5–45° ) angle between the vessel and the 1D scanning beam .
keep_reasoning: Specifies a clear technical constraint that limits complete measurement of total retinal blood flow, important for interpreting results.

fact: Rotating the mouse head by ±30° on an adjustable stage partially addressed the angle problem but vessels that were nearly orthogonal to the scanning beam remained difficult to image.
source_span: While a partial solution for this was implemented by having an additional rotational degree of freedom on the mouse stage , which enable rotating the mouse head and thus the view of the retina by ±30° , vessels which were near orthogonal to the scanning beam still remained challenging to image .
keep_reasoning: Describes an implemented workaround and its limitations, which a lay summary might mention to convey ongoing technical challenges.

fact: Future work will attempt to optically rotate the beam so that all vessels around the optic disk can be measured and provide a more precise total blood flow value.
source_span: Future work will look at optically rotating the beam so that all vessels around the optic disk can be measured to give a more precise value of total blood flow .
keep_reasoning: States a clear next step and improvement direction relevant to the method's future clinical or research utility.

fact: The authors did not use theoretical Poiseuille flow relationships (flow ∝ diameter^3 or diameter^4) to predict flow when velocity could not be measured.
source_span: We refrained from using the theoretical Poiseuille flow relationships ( flow ∝ diameter3 or flow ∝ diameter4 ) to predict flow based on lumen diameter of the first-generation vessels in which velocity could not be measured .
keep_reasoning: Explains a conservative methodological choice that affects how flow is estimated when direct velocity data are missing.

fact: For the most common retinal vessels (tens of microns wide or less), lumen diameter alone is not an accurate predictor of blood flow.
source_span: Our data shows that for the most populous vessels of the mammalian eye , which are tens of microns wide or less , diameter alone is not an accurate predictor of flow ( Figure 10B ) .
keep_reasoning: Key finding that challenges a simple assumption (flow from diameter) and is important for interpreting retinal hemodynamics.

fact: Eye motion minimally affects blood velocity measurements in anesthetized mice.
source_span: Finally , we have demonstrated that eye motion minimally impacts our blood velocity measurements in the anesthetized mouse .
keep_reasoning: Reassures that measurements are reliable under typical anesthetized imaging conditions.

fact: Rapid and saccadic eye movements in awake mice and humans will pose a challenge to the line-scan technique.
source_span: However , rapid and saccadic eye motion in both the awake behaving mouse and the human being will pose a challenge to our line-scan technique .
keep_reasoning: Identifies a realistic limitation for translating the method to awake animals and humans, relevant for clinical applicability.

fact: The challenge of eye motion can be mitigated by restricting analysis to periods of relatively low eye motion (gating out saccades and blinks).
source_span: Such a challenge can be mitigated by restricting the analysis window to epics of relatively low eye motion ( gating out saccades/blinks ) .
keep_reasoning: Provides a practical mitigation strategy that an expert lay summary could report to explain how the problem is handled.

fact: Only a few seconds of contiguous line-scan data per vessel are needed to get reliable hemodynamic measurements; 2–4 seconds will cover multiple cardiac cycles in humans, and the automated algorithm can report velocities from hundreds of thousands of cells.
source_span: Only a few seconds of such line-scan data is needed from each vessel to get a reliable measurement of an array of hemodynamic biomarkers . Even 2–4 s of contiguous data will cover multiple cardiac cycles in the human , and our automated algorithm will be able to report velocities from hundreds of thousands of cells .
keep_reasoning: Highlights the method's efficiency and the scale of data the automated analysis can handle, which supports potential clinical use.

fact: The study demonstrates noninvasive measurement of multiple functional biomarkers in mouse retinal blood vessels ranging from 3 to 46 µm in diameter without using exogenous fluorophores.
source_span: This study has shown that we can noninvasively study an array of functional biomarkers in mouse retinal blood vessels of size 3–46 µm , without using exogenous fluorophores .
keep_reasoning: Central take-home: noninvasive, label-free capability to measure small retinal vessels, crucial for translational relevance.

fact: Microscopic blood vessels contribute a large fraction of the body's total vascular resistance and are often implicated in vascular diseases, but their small size and tissue scattering make them hard to study in vivo.
source_span: These microscopic vessels impart a large fraction of the total resistance to blood flow in the body . Therefore , they are often implicated in many a vascular disease , but their small size , tissue scattering properties and aberrations have made them difficult to study in vivo .
keep_reasoning: Provides medical context for why studying small vessels matters and why new imaging approaches are needed.

fact: The eye is considered a possible 'window to the brain' because the brain is optically inaccessible at high resolution for studying microscopic blood flow.
source_span: It has long been proposed that the eye may serve as a window to the brain . The brain is optically inaccessible with high resolution , especially for studying flow in microscopic vessels .
keep_reasoning: Conceptual background explaining why retinal imaging can give insight into central nervous system microcirculation.

fact: Functional imaging tools for the brain (like fMRI) have millimeter-scale resolution and report bulk blood flow changes as an indirect measure of neuronal activity, not microscopic vessel flow.
source_span: Functional imaging of the brain can today only be done with a resolution of a few millimeters , like in fMRI and other techniques , by reporting bulk changes in blood flow as an indirect measure of neuronal activity .
keep_reasoning: Clarifies the resolution gap between brain imaging and the microscopic vessel-level measurements the retinal approach offers.

fact: The retina's transparency and its status as part of the central nervous system make it a good location to study blood flow behavior in metabolically active neuronal tissue.
source_span: The transparency of the eye and it being a part of the CNS makes it a good location to study the behavior of blood flow in a neuronal tissue with high metabolic demand .
keep_reasoning: Explains why the eye is a practical surrogate for studying CNS microcirculation in a lay-friendly way.

fact: Investigating brain microvasculature typically requires thinned-skull preparations and fluorescent labeling of plasma or red blood cells to measure both velocity and lumen diameter.
source_span: The optical opacity of the brain and scattering in its tissue requires investigation of its microvasculature to need thinned-skull preparations and fluorescent labeling of either plasma or RBCs for measurement of both velocity and lumen diameter ( Drew et al . , 2010; ... ) .
keep_reasoning: Describes why direct brain microvascular imaging is invasive and technically demanding, motivating the retinal alternative.

fact: Techniques that use fluorescent labels or other exogenous blood contrast agents raise concerns about maintaining natural blood perfusion at the capillary level and cannot be applied to humans.
source_span: While all the above techniques have made important advances in our understanding of microcirculation in neural tissues , the use of exogenous blood contrast agents raises the concern of maintenance of natural blood perfusion , especially at the capillary level . Furthermore , such invasive techniques cannot be applied to humans .
keep_reasoning: Highlights safety and translational limitations of labeled/invasive methods, supporting the value of a label-free approach.

fact: Label-free adaptive optics imaging can produce improved contrast of single blood cells in the retina compared to dye-labeling techniques, especially under high flow conditions.
source_span: We have shown recently ( Guevara-Torres et al . , 2016 ) that with label-free adaptive optics imaging , improved contrast of single blood cells can be achieved in the retina , compared to contrast of dye labeling techniques , especially in high flow conditions .
keep_reasoning: Supports the technical advantage of the authors' label-free approach, which a lay summary would emphasize.

fact: The authors suggest their noninvasive retinal method could supplement understanding of CNS microcirculation dynamics and serve as a window to systemic microvascular health.
source_span: Our method of noninvasively studying the retina may serve as a window to supplement the understanding of microcirculation dynamics in the CNS . The eye may also serve as a window to systemic microvascular health .
keep_reasoning: States the broader implication that retinal measurements could inform both brain and whole-body small-vessel health.

fact: Vascular diseases such as diabetes, atherosclerosis, and hypertension affect microscopic vessels throughout the body, which are often hard to study in vivo in organs like the heart and kidneys.
source_span: Vascular diseases like diabetes , atherosclerosis and hypertension are known to impact the microscopic vessels of the body . These tiny vessels often elude in vivo study because of their small size , especially in optically inaccessible areas of the body like the heart , kidneys and other internal organs .
keep_reasoning: Provides clinical motivation for indirect study of systemic microvascular disease via the eye.

fact: The noninvasive nature of this retinal imaging approach and the safe infrared light levels used could make it possible to measure single blood cell flow in humans.
source_span: Finally , the noninvasive nature of this study , and the safe ( infrared ) light levels used , offers the possibility to measure the full spectrum of single blood cell flow in humans ( Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology [Joseph et al . , 2018] ) .
keep_reasoning: States a key translational implication relevant to potential human clinical or research applications.

fact: The experimental study used 19 normal C57BL/6J mice aged 13–73 weeks with a deliberately broad age and sex range to cover the extent of viable blood flow.
source_span: Nineteen normal C57BL/6J mice ( The Jackson Laboratory stock 000664 , Bar Harbor , Maine , USA ) with ages ranging from 13 to 73 weeks old were used in this study ( 11 males , 4 females and four undocumented , weight = 31 . 7 ± 8 . 1 g ( mean ± SD ) ) . In this study of normal mice , a broad age and sex range were intentionally chosen , to cover the extent of the viable blood flow .
keep_reasoning: Provides basic information about the study population and the authors' rationale for their sampling, which helps readers judge generalizability.

fact: The study used nineteen normal C57BL/6J mice aged 13 to 73 weeks (11 males, 4 females, 4 undocumented).
source_span: Nineteen normal C57BL/6J mice ( The Jackson Laboratory stock 000664 , Bar Harbor , Maine , USA ) with ages ranging from 13 to 73 weeks old were used in this study ( 11 males , 4 females and four undocumented , weight = 31 . 7 ± 8 . 1 g ( mean ± SD ) ) .
keep_reasoning: Basic description of the experimental subjects is essential for a lay summary to convey what organism and sample size the findings apply to.

fact: A broad age and sex range of normal mice was intentionally chosen to cover the extent of viable blood flow.
source_span: In this study of normal mice , a broad age and sex range were intentionally chosen , to cover the extent of the viable blood flow .
keep_reasoning: Explains the study design choice and why variability in age/sex mattered for measuring blood flow, which a lay reader needs to understand the motivation.

fact: Mice were housed in standard cages in a vivarium with 12–hour light/dark cycles.
source_span: Mice were housed in standard cages in a vivarium with 12–hour light/dark cycles .
keep_reasoning: Conveys standard animal-care conditions that contextualize the physiological state of the animals.

fact: Mice were fed standard chow and water ad libitum.
source_span: Mice were fed standard chow and water ad libitum .
keep_reasoning: Simple animal-care fact that helps reassure readers the animals were maintained under normal feeding conditions.

fact: Mice were anesthetized in two stages: first by intraperitoneal injection of ketamine/xylazine and then with 0.8–1% isoflurane gas.
source_span: Mice were anesthetized in two stages , first with an intraperitoneal injection ( IP ) of ketamine/xylazine ( 100 mg kg–1 ketamine , 10 mg kg–1 xylazine ) , and second with a gas mixture of 0 . 8–1% ( v/v ) isoflurane .
keep_reasoning: Describes how animals were kept immobile and comfortable during imaging, important context for interpreting in vivo measurements.

fact: Supplemental oxygen was delivered through a nose cone to maintain anesthesia during the imaging sessions.
source_span: Supplemental oxygen was delivered through a nose cone to maintain anesthesia throughout the imaging session , which typically spanned ~2 hr .
keep_reasoning: Explains an important physiological support measure used during in vivo imaging that affects animal stability and data quality.

fact: Pupils were dilated with 2.5% phenylephrine and 1% tropicamide before imaging.
source_span: The pupils were dilated with a drop of 2 . 5% phenylephrine ( Akorn , Lake Forest , Illinois , USA ) and 1% tropicamide ( Sandoz , Basel , Switzerland ) .
keep_reasoning: Dilation is a key preparatory step for retinal imaging and is useful background for lay readers to understand how the eye was imaged.

fact: A custom rigid contact lens with ophthalmic lubricant was used to maintain corneal hydration during in vivo imaging.
source_span: A custom rigid contact lens with +10 D correction and a base curve of 1 . 6 mm ( Advanced Vision Technologies , Lakewood , Colorado , USA ) was used in combination with ophthalmic lubricant ( GenTeal , Alcon Laboratories , Inc , Fort Worth , Texas , USA ) to maintain corneal hydration during in vivo imaging .
keep_reasoning: Explains how the researchers protected the eye and preserved optical quality during prolonged imaging, information a lay summary might include.

fact: The imaging instrument operated in free space with no physical contact to the mouse eye or contact lens to preserve normal ocular pressure dynamics.
source_span: The imaging instrument was in free space , meaning it had no physical contact with the mouse eye or the contact lens . This was critical to maintain normal pressure dynamics of the eye .
keep_reasoning: Highlights an important design choice that prevented artifactually altering eye pressure, relevant to interpreting blood-flow measurements.

fact: A stereotaxic stage with translational and rotational degrees of freedom was used to align the mouse pupil to the imaging system and to navigate and rotate the retinal field of view.
source_span: The three translational degrees of freedom of the stereotaxic stage were used to align the mouse pupil with the exit pupil of the imaging system . Two rotational degrees of freedom were used to navigate to different retinal locations . A third rotational degree of freedom allowed rotating the mouse head along the optical axis , thus enabling rotating the view of the retina at a given retinal location .
keep_reasoning: Explains how precise mechanical positioning enabled targeted retinal imaging, which helps readers understand how different retinal areas were accessed.

fact: In some experiments, blood plasma was labeled by intraperitoneal injection of sodium fluorescein to confirm microvessel lumen diameters measured by label-free phase-contrast methods.
source_span: In a subset of experiments , blood plasma was labelled with an IP injection of 0 . 1 mL of 2 . 5% weight/volume of sodium fluorescein ( AK-FLUOR 10% ( 100 mg mL–1 ) , Akorn , Lake Forest , Illinois , USA ) to confirm lumen diameter of microvessels made with label–free phase-contrast approaches described below .
keep_reasoning: Describes a validation step comparing labeled fluorescence to label-free measurements, which supports the reliability of vessel-size measurements.

fact: The custom-built adaptive optics scanning light ophthalmoscope (AOSLO) used a 904 nm laser diode as the wavefront-sensing beacon.
source_span: A 904 nm laser diode ( QFLD-905–10S , QPhotonics , Ann Arbor , Michigan , USA ) was used as the wavefront sensing beacon .
keep_reasoning: Background about the imaging system; wavefront sensing is central to adaptive optics performance and can be explained in lay terms.

fact: The AOSLO used a 796 nm superluminescent diode for near-infrared reflectance imaging and a 488 nm laser diode to excite sodium fluorescein (with emission collected near 520 nm).
source_span: A 796∆17 nm super luminescent diode ( S790-G-I-15 , Superlum , Ireland ) was used for near infrared reflectance imaging . A 488 nm laser diode ( iChrome MLE , Toptica Photonics , Farmington , New York , USA ) was used as the excitation source for sodium fluorescein ( collected emission: 520∆35 nm; FF01-520/35-25 , Semrock , Rochester , New York , USA ) .
keep_reasoning: Specifies the imaging wavelengths and fluorescence excitation/emission, useful for explaining how blood plasma or structures were visualized.

fact: The AOSLO formed en face retinal images by scanning the illumination point spread function with a slow 25 Hz galvometric scanner and a fast 15 kHz resonant scanner in orthogonal directions.
source_span: An AOSLO images in en face view . At two of the pupil planes in this relay system , a slow 25 Hz galvometric scanner ( VM2500+ , General Scanning , GSI Group Corp . , Massachusetts , USA ) and a fast 15 kHz resonant scanner ( SC30: 15K , Electro--Optical Products Corp . , Glendale , New York , USA ) scanned the illumination point spread function ( PSF ) in orthogonal directions , forming an en face rectangular imaging raster on the retinal image plane .
keep_reasoning: Describes how the imaging system acquires maps of the retinal surface, which is helpful when explaining image formation to non-specialists.

fact: The imaging field of view could be varied between 0.5 and 6.2 degrees, and images were digitized at 640×480 pixels with 8‑bit grayscale depth.
source_span: The field of view in the two orthogonal directions could be independently changed to vary between 0 . 5 and 6 . 2 degrees , and all images were digitized into 640 × 480 pixels with 8–bit grayscale depth .
keep_reasoning: Gives a sense of the scale and digital resolution of the images, which lay readers may find useful to understand image detail.

fact: A high-speed deformable mirror corrected low- and high-order monochromatic aberrations of the mouse eye in real time and provided programmable defocus control to focus on specific retinal vascular layers without additional optics.
source_span: A third pupil plane consisted of a large-stroke high-speed deformable mirror ( DM97-15 , ALPAO , Montbonnot-Saint-Martin , France ) which corrected for low and high order monochromatic aberrations of the eye in real time , measured by a Hartmann-Shack wavefront sensor . The deformable mirror also provided programmable defocus control which enabled focusing the imaging beam on a vascular layer of interest in the retina without using additional optics .
keep_reasoning: Summarizes the adaptive optics capability that enabled clear, layer-specific imaging of retinal blood vessels, a key technical advance relevant to the study.

fact: The confocal design of the imaging system provided tight axial sectioning that rejected out‑of‑focus light and enabled focusing on individual retinal vascular layers (superficial, intermediate, or deep).
source_span: The confocality of our imaging system provided tight axial sectioning of the retina by rejecting out of focus light , enabling tight focusing on only the retinal vascular layer of interest ( superficial , intermediate or deep ) ( Schallek et al . , 2013a ) .
keep_reasoning: Explains how the system could isolate different layers of retinal vasculature, which is central to measuring layer-specific blood flow.

fact: The mouse eye has a larger numerical aperture (NA = 0.49 for a 2 mm dilated pupil) than the human eye (NA = 0.24 for an 8 mm dilated pupil), which improves axial sectioning in mouse retinal imaging.
source_span: The large numerical aperture ( NA ) of the mouse eye further improved axial sectioning ( mouse: NA = 0 . 49 for 2 mm dilated pupil , human: NA = 0 . 24 for 8 mm dilated pupil ) ( Geng , 2011 ) .
keep_reasoning: Provides an explanatory bridge for why high-resolution, layer-specific imaging works particularly well in mice compared with humans.

fact: The system achieved near diffraction-limited in vivo lateral resolution of 1.2 µm for 796 nm reflectance imaging and 0.77 µm for 520 nm fluorescence emission.
source_span: Adapting their measured results by linearly scaling for our imaging wavelengths , the measured in vivo lateral resolution of our system is 1 . 2 µm ( for 796 nm reflectance imaging ) and 0 . 77 µm ( for 520 nm fluorescence emission ) , giving near diffraction limited imaging in vivo .
keep_reasoning: Quantifies the imaging resolution, supporting claims about the ability to resolve small retinal capillaries in live mice—a key point for lay audiences.

fact: The measured in vivo axial resolution of the system was 16.1 µm for 796 nm reflectance imaging and 10.5 µm for 520 nm fluorescence emission.
source_span: The measured axial resolution is 16 . 1 µm ( for 796 nm reflectance imaging ) and 10 . 5 µm ( for 520 nm fluorescence emission ) .
keep_reasoning: Axial resolution numbers support explanations about how well the system can separate different retinal layers in depth.

fact: Animals were allowed to recover from anesthesia after imaging and were returned to their cages for use in future experiments.
source_span: Animals were allowed to recover from anesthesia after imaging and subsequently returned to their cages for use in future experiments .
keep_reasoning: Indicates ethical and logistical treatment of animals after procedures, which may be included in lay summaries addressing animal welfare.

fact: The in vivo lateral resolution of the imaging system is 1.2 µm for 796 nm reflectance imaging and 0.77 µm for 520 nm fluorescence emission, giving near diffraction-limited imaging in vivo.
source_span: Adapting their measured results by linearly scaling for our imaging wavelengths, the measured in vivo lateral resolution of our system is 1.2 µm (for 796 nm reflectance imaging) and 0.77 µm (for 520 nm fluorescence emission), giving near diffraction limited imaging in vivo.
keep_reasoning: Resolution values and the claim of near-diffraction-limited imaging are central to explaining that single-cell retinal imaging is technically feasible.

fact: The measured axial resolution of the imaging system is 16.1 µm for 796 nm reflectance imaging and 10.5 µm for 520 nm fluorescence emission.
source_span: The measured axial resolution is 16.1 µm (for 796 nm reflectance imaging) and 10.5 µm (for 520 nm fluorescence emission).
keep_reasoning: Axial resolution is needed to explain the three-dimensional precision of the imaging and why vessel lumen measurements are accurate.

fact: The optical point spread function (PSF) size is smaller than the 6.7 µm average size of an undeformed mouse red blood cell (RBC).
source_span: The optical point spread function (PSF) size is smaller than the 6.7 µm average size of an undeformed mouse RBC (Gulliver, 1875).
keep_reasoning: Comparing PSF to RBC size shows the system can resolve individual blood cells, an important capability for the study.

fact: The imaging capabilities enabled single blood cell resolution as they flowed in both tight and sparsely packed formations inside microvessels.
source_span: Combined, these imaging capabilities enabled single blood cell resolution as they flowed in both tight and sparsely packed formations inside microvessels (Guevara-Torres et al., 2016).
keep_reasoning: Single-cell resolution in vivo is a core capability that underpins the study's measurements and conclusions.

fact: All flowing cells were imaged noninvasively using near-infrared backscatter without the need for injected dyes.
source_span: All flowing cells were imaged noninvasively with near infrared backscatter, without the need for foreign dye injections.
keep_reasoning: Noninvasive, label-free imaging is important for translational relevance and patient-friendly descriptions.

fact: The high imaging resolution enabled sub-micrometer precision when measuring the lumen diameters of retinal vessels.
source_span: Furthermore, this detailed resolution enabled sub-micrometer precision when measuring the lumen diameters of retinal vessels.
keep_reasoning: Precision of diameter measurement is central to claims about accurately quantifying flow and vessel size.

fact: The study examined 123 retinal vessels in 19 mice.
source_span: In total, 123 vessels in 19 mice were studied.
keep_reasoning: Sample size and study scope provide context for the reliability and scale of the findings.

fact: Eighteen of the studied vessels were primary vessels emerging from the optic disk (first-generation vessels).
source_span: Of these, 18 were primary vessels emerging from optic disk (1st generation vessels),
keep_reasoning: Breakdown by vessel generation helps explain which parts of the retinal circulation were analyzed.

fact: Fifteen studied vessels spanned generations two to five of retinal branching.
source_span: 15 were vessels spanning generations of 2nd to 5th branch order in the retina
keep_reasoning: Specifying mid-sized vessel coverage clarifies the range of vessel types measured.

fact: Ninety of the studied vessels were single-file-flow capillaries.
source_span: and 90 were single file flow capillaries.
keep_reasoning: Large capillary sample emphasizes the study's focus on microcirculation and single-file cell flow.

fact: The authors classified vessels with lumen diameter less than 7 µm as capillaries, using the ~6.7 µm undeformed mouse RBC size as the biological rationale for expecting single-file flow and cell deformation.
source_span: A lumen diameter less than 7 µm was used to categorize a vessel as a capillary, as vessels with lumen diameter below the 6.7 µm undeformed size of a mouse RBC (Gulliver, 1875) are expected to have single-file flow and facilitate cell deformation that is characteristic of capillary exchange vessels.
keep_reasoning: The capillary cutoff and its biological basis are key to interpreting which vessels show single-file flow and exchange behavior.

fact: Measured capillary lumen diameters in the study ranged from 3.2 to 6.5 µm.
source_span: Using this criterion, lumen diameters of capillaries ranged from 3.2 to 6.5 µm.
keep_reasoning: The measured capillary size range supports claims about single-file flow and cell deformation in the retina.

fact: Among vessels larger than 7 µm, 25 were classified as arterioles and eight as venules.
source_span: Of the vessels > 7 µm, 25 were arterioles and eight were venules.
keep_reasoning: Distinguishing arterioles and venules clarifies which vessel types contributed to larger-vessel measurements.

fact: Arterioles and venules were identified by inspecting space–time images to determine whether flow was toward or away from the optic disk.
source_span: Arterioles and venules were identified by inspecting their space-time images to determine direction of flow to or away from the optic disk, as described in detail later.
keep_reasoning: Explaining how vessel type was determined helps readers understand the basis of flow-direction classifications.

fact: Lumen diameters of the identified arterioles and venules ranged from 8.6 to 45.8 µm.
source_span: Their lumen diameters ranged from 8.6 to 45.8 µm.
keep_reasoning: Reporting the diameter range for larger vessels contextualizes the size span of the retinal circulation studied.

fact: Overall, the vessel diameters studied spanned 3.2 to 45.8 µm, covering the smallest to largest vessels in the mouse retinal circulation.
source_span: Taken together, the range of vessel diameters spanned 3.2–45.8 µm, comprising the smallest to largest vessels in the mouse retinal circulation.
keep_reasoning: Summarizing the full diameter range highlights the comprehensiveness of the vascular sampling.

fact: Capillaries in the study belonged to one of three retinal vascular layers, while arterioles and venules were predominantly restricted to the superficial vascular layer.
source_span: Capillaries studied belonged to one of three retinal vascular layers. Arterioles and venules studied were predominantly restricted to the superficial vascular layer.
keep_reasoning: Layer assignment is relevant to retinal anatomy and may affect flow and imaging interpretation.

fact: In arterioles and venules the researchers measured lumen diameter, pulsatile velocity, and flow using oblique-angle scanning.
source_span: In arterioles and venules, lumen diameter, pulsatile velocity and flow were measured using oblique angle scanning (described below).
keep_reasoning: Describing what was measured and the method used is essential to explaining the study's results on larger vessels.

fact: In capillaries the researchers measured average cell velocity and average flow rate using orthogonal scanning, supplementing previously reported lumen diameter and cell flux in single-file-flow capillaries.
source_span: In capillaries, average cell velocity and average flow rate was measured using orthogonal scanning (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and described later), supplementing the lumen diameter and cell flux reported in single-file-flow capillaries in our previous publication (Guevara-Torres et al., 2016).
keep_reasoning: Specifying capillary measurements and technique explains how microcirculatory flow was quantified.

fact: The authors define ‘large’ retinal vessels in the mouse as first-generation vessels near the optic disk that have not yet branched in the retinal plane, with diameters from 45.8 to 20.1 µm.
source_span: For the mouse, we define ‘large’ vessels as first generation vessels near the optic disk, that is vessels that have not yet branched in the retinal plane (diameters: 45.8 to 20.1 µm).
keep_reasoning: Clear vessel-size definitions are needed for an expert lay summary to interpret size-dependent findings.

fact: The authors define ‘medium-sized’ retinal vessels as second-generation and higher vessels that do not have single-file flow, with diameters from 20.1 to 7 µm.
source_span: We define ‘medium-sized’ vessels as vessels from second generation and higher, which do not contain single-file-flow (diameters: 20.1 to 7 µm).
keep_reasoning: This classification explains where transitions from multi-file to single-file flow occur in the vascular tree.

fact: The authors define ‘small’ vessels as capillaries with single-file flow, with diameters from 7 to 3 µm.
source_span: Small vessels are defined as vessels which have single-file-flow, that is capillaries (diameters: 7 to 3 µm) (Guevara-Torres et al., 2016).
keep_reasoning: Provides an explicit size range for capillaries used in the study, relevant to interpreting flow behavior.

fact: The average undeformed size of a mouse red blood cell (6.7 µm) was used as a biologically inspired threshold to identify single-file-flow vessels.
source_span: The average undeformed size of a mouse RBC (6.7 µm) is used as a bio-inspired threshold to identify single-file-flow vessels from others.
keep_reasoning: Explains the biological basis for the capillary cutoff and how cell size informs vessel classification.

fact: Although the vessel-size definitions conceptually hold for the human retina, the largest human retinal vessels are about four times larger than the largest mouse retinal vessels to perfuse a much greater retinal area.
source_span: Conceptually, the above definitions also hold true for the human retina, though the largest human retinal vessels are about four times larger than the largest mouse retinal vessels, to accommodate perfusion for a much greater retinal area.
keep_reasoning: Translates mouse measurements to human scale and explains why absolute sizes differ between species.

fact: Previous seminal laser Doppler and Doppler OCT studies have measured mean velocity down to medium-sized vessels in the human retina.
source_span: By these definitions, seminal laser Doppler and Doppler OCT studies have measured mean velocity down to ‘medium-sized’ vessels in the human retina (Riva et al., 1985; Wang et al., 2007).
keep_reasoning: Positions the new imaging approach relative to earlier human retinal blood flow measurements.

fact: Adaptive optics scanning light ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) retinal imaging in this study used near-infrared illumination centered at 796 nm (±17 nm) with 200–500 µW at the cornea and detected backscattered/reflected light.
source_span: AOSLO retinal imaging was performed using near infrared illumination (796∆17 nm, 200–500 µW at cornea) and detection of backscattered/reflected light.
keep_reasoning: Specifying illumination and detection modality is important to explain the noninvasive, label-free imaging approach.

fact: Two-dimensional en face AOSLO imaging covered a field of view from 0.5° to 5.9° depending on vessel size.
source_span: The two-dimensional (2D) en face imaging spanned 0.5–5.9° field of view, depending on vessel size.
keep_reasoning: Field-of-view details clarify how imaging was adapted to different vessel sizes.

fact: The plane of focus was adjusted to axially bisect the widest portion of each vessel to ensure the maximum luminal width was imaged based on the cylindrical shape of perfused vessels.
source_span: The plane of focus was adjusted to axially bisect the widest portion of the vessel, thus ensuring maximum luminal width was investigated based on cylindrical shape of perfused vessels.
keep_reasoning: Explains how the imaging protocol maximized accurate measurement of vessel diameters.

fact: Most retinal vessels are perpendicular to the imaging optical axis, which makes them suitable for en face imaging with this system.
source_span: Most retinal vessels are perpendicular to the imaging optical axis, making them suitable to study using our en face imaging system.
keep_reasoning: Justifies the choice of en face imaging and why retinal geometry is favorable for the method.

fact: Primary arterioles and venules that dive into the optic disk were imaged between roughly 170 and 300 µm from the center of the optic disk.
source_span: The largest retinal vessels, however, dive into the optic disk. Therefore, when imaging primary arterioles and venules emerging from the optic disk, imaging location was between ~170 and 300 µm from the center of the optic disk.
keep_reasoning: Tells readers where larger vessels were sampled to avoid optic disk geometry complications.

fact: The researchers recorded 4–20 second videos at 25 Hz for 2D imaging and used the average 2D image to analyze vessel geometry and map the vascular tree.
source_span: A 4 to 20 s video (25 Hz, Video 1) was recorded. The average 2D image from the same video was used for analysis of vessel geometry w.r.t. fast scan (angle ϕ in Figure 1B and Equation 1), and to create a map of the vascular tree.
keep_reasoning: Describes the basic data acquisition used to extract geometry and guide subsequent high-speed scans.

fact: To measure high-bandwidth velocities, the slow galvometric scanner was stopped so the fast one-dimensional scan imaged the vessel at 15 kHz.
source_span: To enable high bandwidth velocity measurement, the scan pattern was changed to increase the temporal resolution (Kleinfeld et al., 1998; Zhong et al., 2008). Briefly, the slow galvometric scanner was stopped at a position such that only the fast one-dimensional (1D) scan imaged the vessel at 15 kHz (Figure 1).
keep_reasoning: Explains the high-temporal-resolution strategy that allowed single-cell velocity measurements in fast-flow vessels.

fact: The 1D scan was placed oblique to the vessel so single-cell velocity could be determined in arterioles and venules ranging from the smallest to the largest in the mouse retina.
source_span: This 1D scan was placed oblique to the vessel of interest, to determine single-cell velocity in the smallest to largest arterioles and venules in the mouse retina.
keep_reasoning: Clarifies the scanning geometry used to convert line-scans into single-cell velocities across vessel sizes.

fact: During 1D scanning the mouse head was rotated so the 1D line passed beyond the vessel edges and the angle between the scan line and vessel axis was positioned between 6° and 43°.
source_span: The mouse head was rotated such that the 1D line passed beyond edge to edge of the obliquely oriented vessel, and such that the angle of intersection between 1D scan and vessel axis was between 6 and 43° (angle ϕ in Figure 1B and Equation 1).
keep_reasoning: Specifies the practical alignment constraints required to obtain reliable oblique line-scan velocity measurements.

fact: The intersection angle between the 1D scan and the vessel axis was set manually during imaging and quantitatively confirmed in post-processing using a custom angle-determination algorithm based on the Radon transform.
source_span: This angle was positioned manually by the experimental operator and was quantitatively confirmed in post processing using a custom angle determination algorithm based on the Radon transform (strategy discussed in detail below).
keep_reasoning: Describes how scan geometry was validated, which affects the accuracy of velocity calculations.

fact: The 1D field of view was positioned to traverse the entire luminal diameter so that at least two-thirds of the imaging field covered the vessel.
source_span: The 1D field of view was positioned to traverse the entire luminal diameter whereby least two-thirds of the imaging field covered the vessel (Figure 1B).
keep_reasoning: Ensuring the scan crosses most of the lumen is important for reliable single-cell tracking and diameter-dependent measurements.

fact: The angle of intersection between the 1D scan and the vessel axis was between 6 and 43 degrees.
source_span: and such that the angle of intersection between 1D scan and vessel axis was between 6 and 43° ( angle ϕ in Figure 1B and Equation 1 ) .
keep_reasoning: Specifies the imaging geometry required to measure blood cell velocities and is central to interpreting the space-time images.

fact: The plane of focus for the 1D scan was kept at the same focus as the 2D scan.
source_span: The plane of focus was kept at the same focus as the 2D scan .
keep_reasoning: Explains how the 1D and 2D imaging were aligned to accurately sample the same retinal plane.

fact: The 1D line ranged from 1.2 to 6.2 degrees of visual angle, corresponding to 40.8–210.8 µm on the mouse retina.
source_span: The 1D line ranged from 1 . 2 to 6 . 2 ° of visual angle ( corresponding to 40 . 8–210 . 8 µm on the retina ) .
keep_reasoning: Gives the spatial scale of the measurements so lay readers can appreciate the small retinal distances being imaged.

fact: A conversion factor of 34 µm per degree field of view was used for the mouse retina.
source_span: To determine conversion of pixels to physical retinal coordinates , we used a Ronchi ruling with known grating period and a conversion of 34 µm per degree field of view in the mouse retina ( Schmucker and Schaeffel , 2004 ) .
keep_reasoning: Explains how visual angle was converted into physical retinal distances for quantitative measurements.

fact: Both 1D and 2D data were non-linearly distorted in the fast scan direction because the resonant scanner produces a sinusoidal scan at 15 kHz.
source_span: Both 1D and 2D data were non-linearly distorted in the fast scan direction due to the sinusoidal nature of the 15 kHz resonant scanner .
keep_reasoning: Provides the technical reason for image distortion that the authors needed to correct for accurate velocity measurement.

fact: Video frames were de-warped (de-sinusoided) in real time using a previously published technique.
source_span: Video frames were de-warped ( or de-sinusoided ) in real time using previously published technique ( Yang et al . , 2015 ) .
keep_reasoning: Describes a necessary image-processing step used to correct scanner-induced distortions before analysis.

fact: 2D retinal motion was corrected in post-processing using image cross-correlation, and the registered video stack was averaged to give a high signal-to-noise 2D raster image.
source_span: 2D retinal motion was corrected in post-processing using image cross-correlation . ... The registered video stack was averaged , giving a high signal-to-noise 2D raster image ( Figure 1B ) .
keep_reasoning: Explains how eye/retina motion was handled to produce stable images for structural reference.

fact: Only motion in the direction of the fast scanner could be corrected in 1D images because there was no structural information in the orthogonal dimension.
source_span: Only motion in the direction of the fast scanner could be corrected in 1D images as there was no structural information in the orthogonal dimension .
keep_reasoning: Clarifies a limitation of the 1D imaging approach important for interpreting the precision of motion correction.

fact: Each line-scan sequence was parsed into single time strips of about 40 ms, and eye motion in anesthetized mice is small over this time compared with blood cell motion.
source_span: In each line-scan sequence lasting 1–10 s , the space-time image was parsed into single time strips ~ 40 ms each . Eye motion in the anesthetized mouse has been previously confirmed to be small in this time regime , relative to blood cell motion ( Guevara-Torres et al . , 2016 ) .
keep_reasoning: Provides justification for the temporal segmentation used to detect and correct eye motion without blurring fast-moving blood cells.

fact: Continuous eye motion detection was performed by normalized cross-correlation between a manually selected reference 40 ms strip and overlapping target strips.
source_span: For continuous eye motion detection , normalized cross correlation was performed between a reference strip and overalpping target strips , each 40 ms wide , separated by one pixel each ( 66 µs ) .
keep_reasoning: Describes the practical method used to register short time epochs and remove eye movement artifacts.

fact: Static features such as the vascular wall appear as horizontal lines (zero velocity) in space-time images and were removed by a temporal moving average with a ~10 ms window acting as a high-pass filter.
source_span: Static features such as the vascular wall are manifest as ‘horizontal’ lines in space-time images which represent zero velocity . To remove this signal which could confound blood cell analysis , an intensity moving average of the space-time image was computed in the time dimension with a large time window of ~10 ms . This strategy is a high-pass temporal filter , where velocities slower than 0 . 03 mm s –1 are removed via running background subtraction .
keep_reasoning: Explains how non-moving structures were suppressed so that moving blood cells could be analyzed.

fact: Velocities slower than 0.03 mm s–1 were removed by the running background subtraction (temporal high-pass filter).
source_span: This strategy is a high-pass temporal filter , where velocities slower than 0 . 03 mm s –1 are removed via running background subtraction .
keep_reasoning: Gives a sensitivity threshold of the preprocessing that affects which slow motions are preserved or eliminated.

fact: 1D scanning data were recorded for 1–10 seconds per vessel to capture multiple cardiac cycles, and repeated 1D scans were stacked to produce a space-time image.
source_span: 1D scanning data was recorded for 1–10 s per vessel to capture multiple cardiac cycles . Repeat 1D scans were stacked sequentially to produce a space-time image ( Figure 1D ) .
keep_reasoning: Explains the recording duration and how time-resolved data were combined to analyze pulsatile blood flow.

fact: Red blood cells appear as bright diagonal streaks in space-time images, and the slope of each streak represents the cell's absolute velocity along the vessel.
source_span: RBCs appeared as bright diagonal streaks in such an image as they show their progressive position across the oblique imaging line . The slope of a streak therefore represents an objective measurement of the absolute velocity of each cell according to the equation: ( 1 ) velocitycell = ΔxΔt∗sec⁡ϕ= k∗cot⁡θ∗sec⁡ϕ
keep_reasoning: Connects the visual pattern seen in the images to the physical quantity (cell velocity) that the method measures.

fact: The measured cell velocity depends on the slope of the streak (cot θ) and the intersection angle ϕ according to velocitycell = (Δx/Δt) * secϕ = k * cotθ * secϕ.
source_span: The slope of a streak therefore represents an objective measurement of the absolute velocity of each cell according to the equation: ( 1 ) velocitycell = ΔxΔt∗sec⁡ϕ= k∗cot⁡θ∗sec⁡ϕwhere , velocitycell is the local single-cell velocity ( mm s–1 ) along the direction of vessel flow , ∆x ( mm ) and ∆t ( s ) are the respective spatial and temporal displacements of blood cells , whose ratio is given by the slope of the cell streak , ϕ is the angle of intersection between flow direction and 1D scan , k is equal to the fast scanner frequency ( Hz ) multiplied by the number of millimeters of retinal tissue per pixel , and θ is angle of the cell streak with respect to the space axis in the space-time image .
keep_reasoning: States the mathematical relationship used to convert image-derived slopes and geometry into physical velocities.

fact: In the authors' orientation convention, a more vertical streak corresponds to a faster cell velocity.
source_span: In our orientation convention; the more ‘vertical’ the streak , the faster the cell velocity .
keep_reasoning: Gives an intuitive rule linking streak orientation to speed for interpreting images.

fact: The quadrant of the streak angle θ (0–90° or 90–180°) indicates flow direction toward or away from the optic disk, allowing vessels to be classified as arterioles or venules.
source_span: The quadrant of θ ( 0–90° or 90–180° ) gave the direction of flow to or away from the optic disk , enabling categorization of each vessel as arteriole or venule .
keep_reasoning: Describes how the imaging method can determine flow direction and thus help identify vessel type.

fact: A 1D scan rate of 15 kHz was used to provide a high velocity measurement bandwidth that covers all biologically possible velocities in retinal vessels from largest to smallest.
source_span: A 1D scan rate of 15 kHz was used to have a high velocity measurement bandwidth , covering all biologically possible velocities in the largest to smallest vessels in the mammalian retina .
keep_reasoning: Explains why a fast scan rate was chosen and that it enables measuring the full physiological range of blood speeds.

fact: For a typical ~5° field of view with the given sampling densities, the measurable velocity bandwidth was approximately 0.03 to 1275 mm s–1.
source_span: The velocity measurement bandwidth was therefore 0 . 03–1275 mm s–1 .
keep_reasoning: Provides the numeric range of blood velocities that the method can detect, showing its sensitivity and dynamic range.

fact: To automatically quantify single-cell velocity, each space-time image was divided into small overlapping regions of interest (ROIs) and a single velocity was assigned to each ROI.
source_span: To automatically quantify single-cell velocity , the 1–10 s long space-time image of each vessel was divided into small overlapping regions of interest ( ROIs ) . A single velocity was assigned to each ROI .
keep_reasoning: Describes the core strategy used to obtain localized velocity measurements across the vessel.

fact: ROI size was chosen to encompass the longest RBC streak based on the undeformed size of a mouse red blood cell (6.7 µm).
source_span: ROI size was selected to encompass the ‘longest’ RBC streak seen in space-time images ( undeformed size of a mouse RBC of 6 . 7 µm [Gulliver , 1875] ) .
keep_reasoning: Explains how the spatial sampling for velocity measurements was chosen using a biological size reference.

fact: ROIs were advanced with 75% overlap and were centered every 2–4 µm across the space dimension, corresponding to measurements every 0.25–1.6 µm perpendicular to the vessel lumen after accounting for the oblique angle.
source_span: ROIs were advanced with 75% overlap to capture a continuous measurement of local velocity ( Figure 3A , green boxes ) . The ROIs were centered every 2–4 µm across the space dimension corresponding to a measurement every 0 . 25–1 . 6 µm perpendicular to the vessel lumen when factoring the oblique angle of beam intersection ( secϕ factor in Equation 1 ) .
keep_reasoning: Describes the high spatial sampling strategy used to map velocity across the vessel lumen.

fact: In the time dimension, ROI sizes ranged from 1.6 to 9.4 ms, providing velocity measurements every 0.4–2.3 ms.
source_span: In the time dimension , ROI size ranged from 1 . 6 to 9 . 4 ms , with a measurement provided every 0 . 4–2 . 3 ms .
keep_reasoning: Gives the temporal resolution of the localized velocity measurements, important for capturing pulsatile flow.

fact: The slope of cell streaks in each ROI was determined automatically using a custom algorithm based on the Radon transform.
source_span: To quantify cellular-level velocity , the slope of cell streaks in each ROI was determined automatically using a custom algorithm using the Radon transform ( MATLAB R2017a , Version 9 . 2 , ( with Image
keep_reasoning: States the automated computational method used to extract velocities from the images, which enables high-throughput single-cell measurements.

fact: The intersection angle ϕ was initially positioned manually by the operator and then quantitatively confirmed in post-processing using a custom angle-determination algorithm based on the Radon transform.
source_span: This angle was positioned manually by the experimental operator and was quantitatively confirmed in post processing using a custom angle determination algorithm based on the Radon transform ( strategy discussed in detail below ) .
keep_reasoning: Explains how the critical geometric parameter (angle) was set and verified, affecting velocity calculations.

fact: The ROIs were square in pixel space (25–141 pixels) to facilitate a rotationally symmetric Radon sinugram.
source_span: The ROIs were square in pixel space ( 25–141 pixels ) to facilitate a rotationally symmetric Radon sinugram .
keep_reasoning: Describes a design choice in the analysis that supports the Radon-transform-based slope detection.

fact: The ROIs were centered every 2–4 µm across the space dimension, corresponding to a measurement every 0.25–1.6 µm perpendicular to the vessel lumen when factoring the oblique angle of beam intersection.
source_span: The ROIs were centered every 2–4 µm across the space dimension corresponding to a measurement every 0 . 25–1 . 6 µm perpendicular to the vessel lumen when factoring the oblique angle of beam intersection ( secϕ factor in Equation 1 ) .
keep_reasoning: Spatial sampling density is important for explaining the single-cell spatial resolution of the velocity measurements.

fact: In the time dimension, ROI size ranged from 1.6 to 9.4 ms, with a measurement provided every 0.4–2.3 ms.
source_span: In the time dimension , ROI size ranged from 1 . 6 to 9 . 4 ms , with a measurement provided every 0 . 4–2 . 3 ms .
keep_reasoning: Temporal resolution details support claims about the method's ability to resolve rapid blood-cell movements and cardiac-phase changes.

fact: The Radon transform rotates the input image ROI through a given set of angles and computes the 1D intensity projection of the image for each rotation.
source_span: The Radon transform rotates the input image ROI through a given set of angles and computes the 1D intensity projection of the image for each rotation ( Deans , 2007; Drew et al . , 2010; Bedggood and Metha , 2014; Deneux et al . , 2011; Deneux et al . , 2012; Chhatbar and Kara , 2013 ) .
keep_reasoning: A simple description of the Radon transform helps lay readers understand how angles (and thus velocities) are detected from streaks.

fact: The set of 1D projections is compiled as a 2D sinugram image, where each column in the image is a 1D projection at a given angle.
source_span: The set of 1D projections is compiled as a 2D sinugram image , where each column in the image is a 1D projection at a given angle ( Figure 3B&C ) .
keep_reasoning: Describing the sinogram outcome of the Radon transform links the image-processing step to how an angle is identified.

fact: Each square ROI was cropped circularly before computing its Radon transform to give equal weight to each possible cell orientation angle.
source_span: Each square ROI was cropped circularly before computing its Radon transform , to give equal weight to each possible cell orientation angle .
keep_reasoning: This preprocessing detail explains a step taken to avoid orientation bias when estimating cell slopes.

fact: The projection angle showing maximum intensity standard deviation corresponded to the dominant orientation describing cell velocity.
source_span: The projection angle showing maximum intensity standard deviation corresponded the dominant orientation describing cell velocity in Equation 1 ( Figure 3D ) .
keep_reasoning: This links the image statistic (max standard deviation) to the measured physical quantity (cell velocity orientation).

fact: A linear velocity search space of 0 to 100 mm s–1 with a velocity resolution of 0.1 mm s–1 was used by mapping a trigonometrically scaled angle search space for the Radon transform.
source_span: A linear velocity search space of 0 to 100 mm s–1 , with a velocity resolution of 0 . 1 mm s–1 was used by mapping a trigonometrically scaled angle search space for the Radon transform , using Equation 1 .
keep_reasoning: Stating the velocity range and resolution clarifies the method's capability to detect biologically relevant blood speeds.

fact: For each ROI a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was computed as the ratio of the maximum column standard deviation to the mean column standard deviation of the sinogram image.
source_span: For each ROI ( analysis window ) , a signal-to-noise ratio ( SNR ) was determined to avoid reporting velocities in noise–filled analysis windows . The SNR value was defined as the ratio of the maximum column standard deviation divided by the mean column standard deviation of the sinogram image ( Figure 3D , Equation 3 ) .
keep_reasoning: Defining the SNR metric explains how the algorithm discriminates true streaks from noise.

fact: An empirical SNR threshold of 2.5 was chosen to determine whether a streak angle measurement was reliable, and analysis windows with SNR < 2.5 were excluded.
source_span: We empirically chose a strict threshold of 2 . 5 to determine whether a streak angle measurement was reliable , based on visual inspection of training data sets . ... Analysis windows that contained SNR <2 . 5 were ruled as containing insufficient signal and were not included in subsequent analysis .
keep_reasoning: The reliability cutoff is important for explaining the study's conservative approach to reporting velocities.

fact: A temporal logic gate ignored velocities that deviated beyond one standard deviation from the mean within a local time window spanning twice the ROI length (n = 9 samples).
source_span: In the time dimension , a local window spanning twice the length of an ROI in time was measured for mean and variance of each cell velocity reported in that window ( n = 9 samples ) . Velocities which deviated beyond one standard deviation of the mean velocity were ignored .
keep_reasoning: Temporal consistency filtering helps avoid false positives and is useful to explain robustness of measurements.

fact: The authors justified the temporal logic gate by noting such short intervals (3.2–18.7 ms, less than 6% of a cardiac cycle) are too small to include physiologically relevant fluctuations.
source_span: This logic gate is valid as such intervals in time are too small to include significant fluctuations in time that are physiologically relevant ( 3 . 2–18 . 7 ms , or less than 6% of a cardiac cycle ) .
keep_reasoning: This justification explains why the temporal filter is a reasonable step rather than arbitrary rejection of data.

fact: A spatial logic gate rejected positions across the vessel lumen that met the SNR criteria for fewer than 2% of the total valid SNR hits.
source_span: In the space dimension , a logic gate limited velocity reporting to only the position across the lumen that provided a sufficient number of measurements relative to the total– positions that met the SNR criteria for fewer than 2% of the total valid SNR hits were rejected .
keep_reasoning: Spatial filtering ensured reported velocities came from positions with sufficient repeated measurements, improving reliability.

fact: Combined, the SNR criterion and the space and time logic gates limited analysis to between 3% and 46% of the total searched ROIs, which still represented thousands of independent measurements in a single vessel.
source_span: Combined , the three criteria including SNR ( Equation 3 ) and the space and time logic gates focused the analysis to between 3% and 46% of the total searched ROIs . While this percentage may appear low , it still represents thousands of independent measurements in a single vessel .
keep_reasoning: This conveys the conservative selection strategy while emphasizing the large absolute number of measurements retained.

fact: Space-time images were superimposed with lines oriented at the determined cell angles where line length represents ROI size and color indicates either SNR pass/fail or velocity.
source_span: To augment visual feedback to the user , space-time images were superimposed with lines oriented at determined cell angles ( Figure 3E ) . The length of these lines represents the ROI size . The color indicates one of two metrics: SNR or velocity .
keep_reasoning: Describing the visualization makes it clear how users could verify or interpret automated angle/velocity detections.

fact: To report mean velocity and flow rate across 33 arterioles and venules, 1 s of space-time data was analyzed and velocities from 499 to 25,210 ROIs were reported.
source_span: To report mean velocity and flow rate ( 33 arterioles and venules in Figure 10A&B ) , 1 s of space-time image data was analyzed and velocities from 499 to 25210 ROIs were reported .
keep_reasoning: This provides a concrete example of the data scale used for vessel-level flow measurements.

fact: To compute an average cardiac cycle and velocity profile for an arteriole, 10 s of data were analyzed and velocities from 123,761 ROIs were reported.
source_span: To report the average cardiac cycle and velocity profile as a function of cardiac phase for the arteriole in Figures 4 and 10 s of data was analyzed , and velocities from 123 , 761 ROIs reported .
keep_reasoning: This highlights the large sample size used to derive a high signal-to-noise average cardiac cycle.

fact: The time binning window was set to 15 ms so each cardiac cycle would be sampled 10–27 times for expected heart rates of 150–400 beats per minute, thereby sampling above the Nyquist limit.
source_span: The time binning window was chosen to span 15 ms , to sample each cardiac cycle 10–27 times for an expected heart rate range of 150–400 beats per minute , thus sampling well above the Nyquist limit .
keep_reasoning: Explaining bin size and Nyquist considerations shows the method's adequacy for resolving cardiac-phase dynamics.

fact: The heart rate was measured as the inverse of the average cardiac cycle time period.
source_span: The heart rate was measured reporting the inverse of the average cardiac cycle time period .
keep_reasoning: This links the measured cardiac cycles to a familiar physiological metric (heart rate) relevant for lay readers.

fact: Vascular indices were computed from the average cardiac cycle using vmax, vmin and vmean where Pulsatility Index PI = (vmax - vmin) / vmean and Resistivity Index RI = (vmax - vmin) / vmax.
source_span: The maximum , minimum and mean velocities of the average cardiac cycle ( vmax , vmin and vmean respectively ) were used to compute vascular indices of pulsatility and resistivity according to the formulae: ( 4 ) Pulsatility index PI= vmax-vminvmean ( 5 ) Resistivity index RI= vmax-vminvmax
keep_reasoning: Defining PI and RI shows how velocity waveforms were summarized into clinically relevant vascular metrics.

fact: All cardiac cycles were phase-matched and averaged to produce a high signal-to-noise average cardiac cycle.
source_span: After peaks and troughs of each cardiac cycle were identified , all cardiac cycles were phase-matched and averaged to produce a high signal-to-noise average cardiac cycle ( Figure 4G ) .
keep_reasoning: Describes how the authors improved signal quality to obtain a representative cardiac-cycle velocity waveform, a key preprocessing step that a lay summary may mention.

fact: The authors computed a pulsatility index (PI) from the average cardiac-cycle maximum, minimum and mean velocities using the formula PI = (vmax - vmin) / vmean.
source_span: The maximum , minimum and mean velocities of the average cardiac cycle ( vmax , vmin and vmean respectively ) were used to compute vascular indices of pulsatility and resistivity according to the formulae: ( 4 ) Pulsatility index PI= vmax-vminvmean ( 5 ) Resistivity index RI= vmax-vminvmax
keep_reasoning: Defines a vascular metric (PI) that summarizes how much blood velocity varies over a heartbeat, which is useful for lay explanations of vascular dynamics.

fact: The authors computed a resistivity index (RI) from the average cardiac-cycle maximum and minimum velocities using the formula RI = (vmax - vmin) / vmax.
source_span: The maximum , minimum and mean velocities of the average cardiac cycle ( vmax , vmin and vmean respectively ) were used to compute vascular indices of pulsatility and resistivity according to the formulae: ( 4 ) Pulsatility index PI= vmax-vminvmean ( 5 ) Resistivity index RI= vmax-vminvmax
keep_reasoning: Defines another standard vascular index (RI) that relates peak-to-trough velocity change to peak velocity, relevant for interpreting vessel resistance.

fact: The authors defined an asymmetry index (AI) for the average cardiac cycle using the time positions of the maximum and two minimum velocities as AI = (tmin2 - tmax) / (tmax - tmin1).
source_span: The time positions of the maximum and two minimum velocities ( tmax , tmin1 and tmin2 respectively , orange and green points in Figure 4G ) were used to compute a custom metric of asymmetry in the profile of the average cardiac cycle: ( 6 ) Asymmetry index ( AI ) = tmin2−tmaxtmax−tmin1
keep_reasoning: Introduces a custom metric that quantifies asymmetry of the velocity waveform across a heartbeat, which could be explained to readers as a measure of waveform shape.

fact: Measured velocities in a single vessel were reported as a velocity profile along the vessel lumen by averaging, across time, all measures performed at a specific radial location.
source_span: Measured velocities in a single vessel were reported as a function of position along the vessel lumen ( velocity profile ) by averaging , across time , all measures performed at a specific radial location .
keep_reasoning: Explains how the authors summarized spatial variation of flow across a vessel, a concept useful for lay descriptions of flow profiles.

fact: The spatial binning window for velocity profiles was chosen to be 4 µm, which corresponds to intervals of 0.77 µm across the vessel lumen when factoring vessel angle.
source_span: The spatial binning window was chosen to be 4 µm , which corresponds to intervals of 0 . 77 µm across the vessel lumen when factoring vessel angle ( Figure 4H and Figure 6 ) .
keep_reasoning: Gives the spatial resolution used to compute velocity profiles, which helps explain how finely the authors sampled flow across vessel cross-sections.

fact: Instantaneous velocity profiles were phase-locked to the cardiac cycle to reveal dependence of the profile on cardiac phase.
source_span: Additionally , instantaneous velocity profiles were phase locked to the cardiac cycle to reveal dependence of the profile on cardiac phase ( Figure 4H and Video 3 ) .
keep_reasoning: Indicates that the study examined how the shape of the flow profile changes during the heartbeat, an important physiological point for lay readers.

fact: The measured velocity profiles were fit with several models of blood flow.
source_span: The measured profiles were fit with several models of blood flow ( Figure 6B ) .
keep_reasoning: Summarizes that the authors compared observed flow shapes to theoretical models, a common approach to interpret flow data in accessible terms.

fact: All flow models assumed symmetric flow by constraining the fit to the position of maximum measured velocity and using an equal number of data points on each side of it.
source_span: Symmetric flow was assumed in all models by constraining the fit to the position of maximum measured velocity , and an equal number of data points to each side of it .
keep_reasoning: States a modeling assumption that affects interpretation of flow profiles and that a lay summary might mention when explaining model limitations.

fact: The red blood cell (RBC) flow profile was modeled using a blunted profile described by Zhong et al. (2011) with parameters including centerline velocity (Vmax), vessel radius (R), an edge-velocity factor (β), and a bluntness index (B).
source_span: The RBC flow profile was modelled as described by Zhong et al . ( 2011 ) . ( 7 ) V ( r ) = Vmax1-1-β . rRBwhere , V ( r ) is velocity at radial position r in a vessel , R is the maximum radial position ( half of measured lumen diameter ) , Vmax is the maximum velocity ( or centerline velocity , assuming symmetric flow ) , β is a custom factor that is proportional to the normalized extrapolated RBC velocity at the lumen edges , and B is a custom bluntness index .
keep_reasoning: Explains the type of flow profile used to represent RBC motion and the key parameters, which can be paraphrased for non-specialists (e.g., 'blunted' vs parabolic flow).

fact: The plasma velocity profile was modeled assuming zero velocity at the lumen edges to satisfy the no-slip boundary condition.
source_span: Additionally , the plasma velocity profile was modeled assuming zero velocity at the lumen edges , to satisfy the no-slip boundary condition ( Figure 6B ) .
keep_reasoning: States a basic physical boundary condition used in modeling blood plasma flow that a lay summary can explain as 'blood near the vessel wall is stationary'.

fact: The authors previously reported label-free measurement of single-cell flux (cells s–1) in capillaries with single-file flow.
source_span: In a previous publication , we reported label-free measurement of single-cell flux ( cells s–1 ) in capillaries with single-file flow ( Guevara-Torres et al . , 2016 ) ( Figure 1—figure supplement 1 ) .
keep_reasoning: Provides background that the team has an established method for counting single red blood cells in single-file capillaries, relevant for interpreting current capillary measurements.

fact: To compare single-cell flux to larger-vessel flow rates, the authors measured average cell velocity from 1 s long space-time images of 90 capillaries captured with split-detection phase contrast.
source_span: To compare those measurements with flow rate ( µL min–1 ) measurements of larger vessels in this current study , we measured the average cell velocity from 1 s long space-time images of 90 capillaries captured with split detection phase contrast ( Figure 10C ) .
keep_reasoning: Explains how capillary measurements were acquired and linked to flow rate estimates, a practical detail useful for readers to understand sample size and measurement approach.

fact: To determine cell velocity in capillaries, cell locations were marked and phase-registered to produce an 'average cell'.
source_span: To determine cell velocity , cell locations were marked and were phase registered to produce an ‘average cell’ .
keep_reasoning: Describes the averaging method used to estimate cell speed from noisy data, which can be explained simply in a lay summary.

fact: Capillary mean velocity was calculated as velocity_mean = d / Δt, where Δt is the temporal width of the average cell and d is the average length of red blood cells along the direction of flow.
source_span: The temporal width of this average cell was used to report average capillary velocity using the equation reported by us previously ( Guevara-Torres et al . , 2016 ) . ( 8 ) velocitymean= d∆twhere ∆t is the temporal width of the average cell , and d is the average length of RBCs along the direction of flow .
keep_reasoning: Gives the simple relationship used to convert measured cell appearance time into a velocity, which can be paraphrased for lay readers.

fact: Red blood cells deform during single-file flow, typically having a long-to-short axis ratio of about 2:1.
source_span: RBCs deform during single-file flow , with a typical long-to-short axis ratio of 2:1 .
keep_reasoning: Provides physiological detail about RBC shape in capillaries that helps explain why an average RBC length must be assumed when computing velocity.

fact: Considering RBC deformation and a mean plasma layer of ~0.5 µm, previous glass-tube studies reported mean RBC lengths ranging from 4.5 to 10 µm across various capillary inner diameters.
source_span: Considering this deformation and a mean plasma layer of ~0 . 5 µm , mean RBC lengths ranging from 4 . 5 to 10 µm were reported in a capillary glass tube study ( Hochmuth et al . , 1970 ) across a variety of capillary inner diameters .

source_span: We have considered two different models to explain how RNAi-mediated depletion of these dynein ACs can suppress reduced HC function . First , these dynein subunits could be in functional complexes with , and exert negative regulation on , the DHC-1 HC ( Figure 5B ) . The other , nonsuppressing , accessory subunits might then function in nonmitotic cellular processes such as neuronal transport or organelle positioning . ... Alternatively , an assortment of dynein complexes ( with different ACs ) could coexist within early embryonic cells , with only a subset required for the essential mitotic functions that require DHC-1 . In this case , suppression might result from the release of DHC-1 HCs from less essential motor complexes , allowing more of the functionally compromised HCs to participate in the essential process of mitosis .
