fact: Nine genomic features are linked with genetic variability, and six of these independently correlated with substitution rates in both MMR-deficient tumors and germ-line genomes.
source_span: At the large-scale level, nine genomic features are linked with genetic variability (Hodgkinson and Eyre-Walker, 2011). Each of these features correlated significantly with substitution frequencies in MMR-deficient tumors and germ-line genomes. Linear modeling revealed that six of these independently correlated with substitution rates in MMR-deficient tumors as well as with germ-line substitutions (Figure 2E).
keep_reasoning: Identifies that multiple independent genomic factors shape mutation rates similarly in MMR-deficient tumors and germ-line variation, strengthening the connection between the two.

fact: The types and context-dependencies of substitutions are largely shared between germ-line and MMR-deficient genomes, suggesting that many human genetic variants arise from mismatches that escape mismatch repair.
source_span: Overall, the types as well as the narrow and broad context-dependencies of substitutions thus appear to be largely shared between germ-line and MMR-deficient genomes, suggesting that a considerable fraction of human genetic diversity arises through mismatches escaping MMR.
keep_reasoning: This is a major take-home implication linking tumor biology to the origins of normal human genetic variation.

fact: Replication timing correlated with transitions but not with transversions in all three MMR-deficient tumors studied.
source_span: First, replication timing correlated with transitions but not transversions in all three MMR-deficient tumors (Figure 2F).
keep_reasoning: Reiterates a reproducible association across multiple MMR-deficient tumors that helps explain mutation distribution.

fact: In other (MMR-proficient) genomes, transversions increase in late S phase, suggesting reduced DNA repair fidelity in late S phase for MMR-proficient cells.
source_span: This contrasts with the increase in late S phase transversions observed in all other genomes studied here (Figure 2F), as well as in lymphoblastoid cell lines (Koren et al., 2012). The increase in MMR-proficient but not MMR-deficient cells suggests a reduced fidelity of DNA repair in late S phase, leading to an increase in transversions.
keep_reasoning: Explains a potential cell-cycle–dependent difference in repair fidelity that affects mutation types in MMR-proficient cells.

fact: DNA repair fidelity in MMR-deficient cells is uniformly low and therefore not affected by replication timing.
source_span: In contrast, DNA repair fidelity in MMR-deficient cells is invariably low and therefore not affected by replication time.
keep_reasoning: Helps explain why MMR-deficient tumors lack the late S phase transversion increase seen in other genomes.

fact: Substitutions are enriched next to simple repeats: bases immediately flanking simple repeats show a 1.6-fold increase in substitutions, with a threefold increase next to homopolymers and a 1.3-fold increase next to microsatellites.
source_span: Indeed, a 1 . 6-fold increase in substitutions at bases immediately flanking simple repeats was noted, with a threefold increase next to homopolymers and a 1 . 3-fold increase next to microsatellites (Figure 2G).
keep_reasoning: Quantifies how repetitive DNA sequences increase the local mutation rate, a mechanistic detail useful for lay explanation.

fact: Most substitutions adjacent to repeats convert the flanking base to the base that composes the repeat, consistent with polymerase slippage.
source_span: These substitutions for the vast majority converted the base flanking the repeat, to the base constituting the repeat (Figure 2G). They are thus probably the result of polymerase slippage events, following a mechanism akin to the previously described bacterial dislocation mutagenesis (Kunkel and Soni, 1988).
keep_reasoning: Provides a mechanistic explanation (polymerase slippage) for why repeats promote specific mutations.

fact: G:C>A:T transitions at CpG sites largely reflect spontaneous, replication-independent deamination of methylated cytosines and depend on CpG content but are inversely correlated with the fraction of CpG islands.
source_span: G:C>A:T transitions in CpG sites strongly depend on CpG content, but are inversely correlated with the fraction of CpG islands (Figure 2E). Spontaneous, replication-independent deaminations of methyl-C to T underlie such transitions.
keep_reasoning: Explains a well-known biochemical source of a common mutation type and its genomic distribution.

fact: MMR-deficient tumors show a much larger increase in CG>TG transitions (3449) than MMR-proficient tumors (145), indicating that replication-independent mismatch repair contributes to deamination repair in vivo.
source_span: Here, the much larger increase in CG>TG transitions observed in MMR-deficient compared to MMR-proficient tumors (3449 vs 145) demonstrates that replication-independent MMR, recently described at the molecular level (Shell et al., 2007; Pena-Diaz et al., 2012), is also involved in deamination repair in vivo (Chen et al., 2014).
keep_reasoning: Connects the observed mutation counts to a specific repair process acting on deaminated methylcytosines in living tissues.

fact: Bases outside CpG islands are nearly twice as likely to undergo substitution as bases inside CpG islands, suggesting DNA methylation contributes to mutagenesis.
source_span: Indeed, irrespective of dinucleotide context, bases outside CpG islands were nearly two times more likely to undergo mutation than those inside CpG islands (Figure 2H). As CpG islands are generally unmethylated, DNA methylation thus appears to contribute to the mutagenic process.
keep_reasoning: Links CpG island methylation status to overall mutation likelihood, an important background point for lay summaries.

fact: Somatic indels in MMR-deficient tumors strongly correlate with simple repeats and are predominantly 1–2 base pairs in length.
source_span: As expected, since the majority of indels was located in homopolymers, a strong correlation between simple repeats and indel frequency was observed (Figure 3A). Indels were also predominantly 1 or 2 bps in length (Figure 3B).
keep_reasoning: Describes the common size and genomic context of insertion/deletion events in MMR-deficient tumors, relevant for explaining microsatellite instability.

fact: Although C or G homopolymers make up a minority of homopolymers (7%), an even smaller fraction of indels affected C:G homopolymers (1.9%), suggesting C:G homopolymers are less likely to accumulate indels.
source_span: Although the minority of homopolymers consists of C or G bases (7%), an even smaller fraction of indels affected C:G homopolymers (1 . 9%; Figure 3C), suggesting that C:G homopolymers are less likely to accumulate indels.
keep_reasoning: This nuanced observation may inform explanations about sequence-specific susceptibility to indels.

fact: Deletions were much more frequent than insertions among indels in MMR-deficient tumors (81% deletions vs 19% insertions), consistent with DNA polymerases being more prone to remove than to add a base during synthesis.
source_span: As observed in other MMR-deficient tumors and also in MMR-deficient Caenorhabditis elegans (Denver et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2013), deletions were remarkably more frequent than insertions (81% vs 19%), confirming that DNA polymerases are more prone to remove than to add a base during DNA synthesis.
keep_reasoning: Gives a clear, mechanistic asymmetry in how indels arise that is useful for lay explanations of mutation processes.

fact: C:G homopolymers make up a minority of homopolymers (7%), and an even smaller fraction of indels affected C:G homopolymers (1.9%), suggesting C:G homopolymers are less likely to accumulate indels.
source_span: Although the minority of homopolymers consists of C or G bases ( 7% ) , an even smaller fraction of indels affected C:G homopolymers ( 1 . 9%; Figure 3C ) , suggesting that C:G homopolymers are less likely to accumulate indels .
keep_reasoning: This directly states a specific sequence-context bias in where indels happen, which a lay summary would use to explain which DNA sequences are more or less vulnerable.

fact: In MMR-deficient tumors (and in MMR-deficient Caenorhabditis elegans), deletions were much more frequent than insertions (81% vs 19%), indicating DNA polymerases are more prone to remove than to add a base during DNA synthesis.
source_span: As observed in other MMR-deficient tumors and also in MMR-deficient Caenorhabditis elegans ( Denver et al . , 2005; Kim et al . , 2013 ) , deletions were remarkably more frequent than insertions ( 81% vs 19% ) , confirming that DNA polymerases are more prone to remove than to add a base during DNA synthesis .
keep_reasoning: This is a core mechanistic finding about the type of errors that accumulate in mismatch-repair (MMR) deficiency and helps explain the mutational pattern.

fact: Substitutions located near somatic indels were enriched within ~30 base pairs, and substitutions near other substitutions were enriched within ~200 base pairs, while substitutions near repeats were enriched only at the base immediately flanking the repeat.
source_span: The substitutions located nearby indels and substitutions were enriched respectively within a range of ∼30 bp and ∼200 bp , whereas substitutions near repeats were enriched only at the base immediately flanking the repeat .
keep_reasoning: This spatial relationship between different mutation types helps explain clustering of mutations and could be used in a summary to describe local effects of mutation processes.

fact: The study analyzed 13 additional MMR-deficient tumors and four MMR-proficient tumors collected from endometrium, colon, and ovarium.
source_span: Next , we selected 13 additional MMR-deficient tumors , as well as four MMR-proficient tumors , collected from different tissues ( i . e . , endometrium , colon , and ovarium ) .
keep_reasoning: A lay summary should state what types and how many human tumor samples were compared to give context for the findings.

fact: Six of the tumor samples were primary tumor cultures of low passage, which the authors preferred over established cell lines because cell lines can develop a hypermutator phenotype and no longer represent the original tumor.
source_span: Of these , six represented primary tumor cultures of low passage , which we preferred over cell lines , because the latter due to their hypermutator phenotype are no longer representative of the original tumor ( Figure 4—source data 2 ) .
keep_reasoning: Explaining the choice of primary cultures over cell lines helps a lay reader understand why the samples better reflect real tumors.

fact: Exome sequencing of tumor and matched germ-line DNA showed each MMR-deficient tumor had about 2,015 somatic events compared to 39 in MMR-proficient tumors, a 52-fold increase.
source_span: Exome-sequencing of tumor and matched germ-line DNA at an average coverage of 44x revealed that each MMR-deficient tumor contained ∼2015 somatic events vs 39 for MMR-proficient tumors ( 52-fold increase; Figure 4A , Figure 4—source data 1 , Figure 4—source data 2 ) .
keep_reasoning: This quantifies the dramatic increase in mutation burden caused by MMR deficiency, a central translationally relevant result.

fact: Validation rates for detected somatic substitutions and indels were 87% and 86%, respectively.
source_span: Validation rates for substitutions and indels were respectively 87% and 86% .
keep_reasoning: Validation rates indicate the reliability of the mutation calls and are important for assessing confidence in the study's results.

fact: Clustering analysis of the 13 MMR-deficient tumors based on genes affected by coding-region substitutions or indels showed no obvious subgroups by cancer type or by primary tumor versus cell culture.
source_span: Clustering analysis of all 13 MMR-deficient tumors for the genes affected by either a somatic substitution or indel in the coding regions revealed no obvious subgroups in terms of cancer of origin or between primary tumors and cell cultures ( Figure 4—figure supplement 1 ) .
keep_reasoning: This suggests the mutational patterns are broadly similar across tissues and sample types, a useful summary point about generality.

fact: Exonic substitutions outnumbered indels in the MMR-deficient exome data, similar to observations in the MMR-deficient whole-genomes.
source_span: Presumably , because of negative clonal selection and differences in homopolymer content in exons vs other genomic regions , exonic substitutions outnumbered indels ( Figure 4A , Figure 4—figure supplement 2 ) , similar to what we observed in the MMR-deficient whole-genomes ( Figure 1C , D ) .
keep_reasoning: Reporting that substitutions dominate in exons helps explain how mutation types differ by genomic region, relevant for understanding which mutations affect protein-coding genes.

fact: Only a minority of indels affected microsatellites, confirming that homopolymers (single-nucleotide repeats) were most frequently affected by indels.
source_span: Only a minority of these indels affected microsatellites , confirming that homopolymers were most frequently affected by indels .
keep_reasoning: This clarifies which repetitive DNA sequences are the main hotspots for indels in MMR-deficient tumors, useful for explaining mechanisms and potential diagnostic markers.

fact: No obvious difference was observed between MLH1-, MSH2-, and MSH6-deficiency in mutation frequencies, substitution patterns, or indel compositions.
source_span: No obvious difference was observed between MLH1- , MSH2- , and MSH6- deficiency in terms of the mutation frequencies , substitution patterns , and indel compositions ( Figure 4—figure supplement 5 ) .
keep_reasoning: This indicates that loss of different MMR genes produces similar mutational consequences, relevant for grouping MMR-deficient cancers clinically.

fact: Indels mainly affected homopolymers (59.0%), while microsatellites and short homopolymers were affected at frequencies expected from their genome-wide occurrence.
source_span: Indels mainly affected homopolymers ( 59 . 0% ) , whereas microsatellites and short homopolymers were affected at a frequency that was expected based on their genome-wide occurrence .
keep_reasoning: This quantifies the concentration of indels in long homopolymers and contrasts it with other repeat types, a summary-worthy pattern.

fact: Indels were depleted in non-repeat regions of the exome.
source_span: In contrast , indels were depleted in non-repeat regions .
keep_reasoning: Noting depletion in non-repeat regions helps explain that indels are concentrated in repetitive DNA rather than spread uniformly, an important conceptual point.

fact: Somatic substitutions affected exonic sequences independently of repeat composition.
source_span: Substitutions affected the exome independent of repeat composition .
keep_reasoning: This contrasts substitution distribution with indels and helps explain different mechanisms and consequences for mutations in coding regions.

fact: Among 477 homopolymers affected in at least 2 of 16 tumors, 176 were A stretches, 135 were T stretches, 85 were G stretches, and 81 were C stretches.

source_span: The observed and expected frequencies of indels recurrently affected in homopolymers ( in at least 2 out of 16 tumors ) stratified for homopolymer length ... The difference between observed and expected recurrent indels is high for short homopolymers , but non-existent for long homopolymers .
keep_reasoning: Indicates that short repeats are unusually prone to recurrent indels beyond what length alone would predict, a key mechanistic observation.

fact: Exomes from tumors deficient for MLH1, MSH2, or MSH6 showed no obvious differences in overall mutation patterns.
source_span: Mutation patterns obtained from MLH1-deficient , MSH2-deficient , and MSH6-deficient exomes . ... No obvious difference is observed .
keep_reasoning: Summarizes that different MMR gene defects produce similar mutation signatures, simplifying interpretation for readers.

fact: In 16 MMR-deficient tumors, 1.6% of homopolymers were recurrently affected by an indel: 2,244 of 29,663 homopolymers were affected at least once and 477 were affected at least twice.
source_span: Remarkably , 1 . 6% of homopolymers was recurrently affected by an indel in the 16 MMR-deficient tumors ... ( i . e . , 2244 out of 29 , 663 homopolymers were affected at least once , whereas 477 were affected at least twice; Figure 4—figure supplement 3 ) .
keep_reasoning: Quantifies how common indels in homopolymers are in MMR-deficient tumors, an important summary metric for lay audiences.

source_span: In contrast , only 55 substitutions were recurrent , three of which were found in ≥2 tumors ( i . e . , two substitutions affecting KRAS codon 12 and 13 were found in three and four tumors ... , whereas a substitution in ZNF648 affected three tumors ).

fact: Long homopolymers (>10 base pairs) are more frequent in untranslated regions (UTRs) than in coding regions.
source_span: When comparing homopolymer content of coding regions vs UTRs , long homopolymers ( >10 bps ) were more frequent in UTRs than in coding regions ( Figure 4B ) .
keep_reasoning: Explains a structural genomic difference that helps account for where indels accumulate, useful background for readers.

fact: Because long homopolymers are more frequently affected, the overall indel rate is lower in coding regions than in UTRs.
source_span: Because these long homopolymers were also more frequently affected ( Figure 4C ) , the overall indel rate in coding regions was lower than in UTRs ( Figure 4D ) .
keep_reasoning: Connects homopolymer distribution to functional regions, clarifying why coding regions have fewer indels overall.

source_span: As a consequence of this difference , recurrent indels also occurred more frequently in UTRs than coding regions ( 31 , 438 vs 1337; Figure 4—source data 3 ) .
keep_reasoning: A direct consequence of the previous facts that is likely to appear in a lay summary about mutation distribution.

source_span: Remarkably , however , recurrent indels were more frequently observed than expected based on indel frequency in short , but not in long homopolymers ( Figure 4E , Figure 4—figure supplement 4 ) . This suggests that features other than homopolymer length underlie indel recurrence rates . Positive clonal selection of indels affecting short homopolymers , which are predominant in coding regions , represents a possible explanation .
keep_reasoning: Proposes a biological explanation (selection) for the observed recurrence pattern, a key interpretation for readers.

fact: Repeating the analysis on only the 13 whole-exome samples produced very similar results, indicating that including exonic mutations from whole-genome sequences did not bias the findings.

keep_reasoning: Supports the robustness of the findings across sequencing strategies, which is useful methodological reassurance for readers.

fact: The extended Bethesda panel, currently used to diagnose microsatellite instability (MSI), consists of eight microsatellite and two homopolymer markers.
source_span: The extended Bethesda panel , which consists of eight microsatellite and two homopolymer markers , is currently used to diagnostically assess MSI ( Pinol et al . , 2005 ) .
keep_reasoning: Provides necessary background about the standard clinical MSI test that the study seeks to improve.

fact: The Bethesda panel was compiled from a limited set of variable markers that are long and variable, making them difficult to analyze and leading to reduced sensitivity for detecting MSI.
source_span: This panel was historically compiled from a limited set of markers known to be variable . Due to their length and variability , these markers are notoriously difficult to analyze and interpret . As a consequence , the Bethesda panel has reduced sensitivity to detect MSI .
keep_reasoning: Explains why a new MSI test might be needed, an important motivation for lay summaries.

fact: To improve MSI testing, the authors selected 59 recurrent indels found in at least 6 of 16 tumors; 50 markers were in 5′ or 3′ UTRs and 9 were in coding regions, and each marker was present in both MMR-deficient endometrial and colorectal cancers.
source_span: In an effort to improve MSI testing , we randomly selected 59 recurrent indels affecting ≥6 out of 16 tumors; 50 markers were in 5′ or 3′UTRs and 9 were in coding regions ( Figure 5—source data 1 ) . Furthermore , each of the markers was detected in both MMR-deficient EM and CRC .
keep_reasoning: Describes the new test design and its applicability to two cancer types, central to the translational message.

fact: The maximal homopolymer length in the 59-marker panel was restricted to 12 base pairs to facilitate high-throughput genotyping.
source_span: To facilitate high-throughput genotyping , the maximal length of affected homopolymers was restricted to 12 bps .
keep_reasoning: Explains a practical design choice that makes the new test more scalable and reliable for clinical use.

fact: Applying the 59-marker panel to 236 endometrial tumors with MMR immunohistochemistry (IHC) data, the authors set a threshold of three positive markers to define MSI, which gave ~98% sensitivity (40/41) and >99% specificity (1/184 false positive) relative to IHC.
source_span: First , we applied these 59 markers to a discovery set of 236 EM tumors for which MMR immunohistochemistry ( IHC ) data were available . This allowed us to determine three positive markers as the threshold with the best Matthew correlation coefficient to detect MMR-deficiency based on IHC and thus to define MSI ( Figure 5A , B ) . At this threshold , our markers detected 40 out of 41 tumors MMR-deficient on IHC ( sensitivity ∼98% ) , while only 1 out of 184 MMR-normal tumors on IHC were identified as MSI ( specificity > 99% ) .
keep_reasoning: Gives key performance metrics showing the new panel's high accuracy against an established clinical reference.

fact: In an independent validation of 114 endometrial tumors, every tumor classified as MSI by the Bethesda panel was also MSI by the 59-marker panel, while 12 tumors were positive only in the 59-marker panel; IHC on nine discordant cases confirmed all nine were MMR-deficient, indicating the 59-marker panel is more sensitive than Bethesda.
source_span: Briefly , each MSI tumor on Bethesda ( >2 markers positive ) was also MSI with the 59-marker panel ( Figure 5C ) . However , 12 tumors were positive in the 59-marker panel , but negative in Bethesda . IHC on the nine discordant tumors for which a paraffin block was available confirmed that each of them was MMR-deficient either for MLH1 or MSH2 , indicating that the 59-marker panel has a higher sensitivity compared to Bethesda .
keep_reasoning: Demonstrates improved clinical sensitivity of the new marker panel over the standard test, a central translational conclusion.

fact: A threshold of 3 markers produced the highest Matthew Correlation Coefficient (MCC = 0.97) on the ROC curve for the classifier.
source_span: ( B ) The Matthew Correlation Coefficient ( MCC ) of the ROC curve was calculated for each threshold , and a threshold of 3 resulted in the highest MCC-value ( MCC = 0 . 97 ) .
keep_reasoning: This identifies the optimal scoring threshold used to call MSI and demonstrates the classifier's high discriminative performance.

fact: The extended Bethesda panel and a 59-marker microsatellite instability (MSI) panel were compared in an independent series of 114 unselected primary endometrial tumors and 126 stage II or III colorectal cancer (CRC) tumors.
source_span: ( C and D ) The extended Bethesda panel and the 59-marker panel were compared in an independent series of 114 unselected primary endometrial tumors ( C ) and 126 stage II or III CRC tumors ( D ) .
keep_reasoning: States the main comparative experiment and the clinical sample sizes used to evaluate the new panel versus the standard Bethesda panel.

fact: Using the 59-marker panel, 71 of 114 endometrial tumors (62%) were classified as microsatellite stable or MSI-low (MSS/MSI-L) and 43 tumors (38%) as MSI-high (MSI-H).
source_span: For endometrial tumors , 71 tumors ( 62% ) were defined as MSS/MSI-L and 43 tumors ( 38% ) as MSI-H by the 59-marker panel .
keep_reasoning: Gives the prevalence of MSI calls in the endometrial tumor cohort using the new panel, which is important for interpreting diagnostic sensitivity.

fact: Of the 43 endometrial tumors called MSI-H by the 59-marker panel, the Bethesda panel identified 32 as MSI-H (>2 markers positive), 7 as MSI-L, and 5 as MSS.
source_span: Out of these 43 MSI-H tumors , Bethesda identified 32 tumors as MSI-H ( >2 markers positive ) , 7 tumors as MSI-L , and 5 tumors as MSS .
keep_reasoning: Shows the concordance and discrepancies between the new panel and the standard Bethesda panel in endometrial cancers.

fact: The Bethesda panel did not identify any MSI-H tumor that was missed by the 59-marker panel in the endometrial tumor set.
source_span: Vice versa , Bethesda did not identify any MSI-H tumor that was not identified by our panel .
keep_reasoning: Indicates that the 59-marker panel captured all MSI-H cases detected by Bethesda, supporting its sensitivity.

fact: In colorectal tumors, 97 tumors called MSS by the 59-marker panel were concordantly called MSS or MSI-L by the Bethesda panel.
source_span: For colorectal tumors , there were 97 MSS tumors in our 59-marker panel that were concordantly called MSS or MSI-L by the Bethesda panel .
keep_reasoning: Demonstrates concordant negative calls between the two panels in colorectal cancer, relevant for specificity.

fact: In the colorectal set, 29 samples were detected as MSI by the 59-marker panel; 28 of these were also called MSI-H by the Bethesda panel, while one was called MSS by Bethesda.
source_span: The remaining 29 samples were detected as MSI in the 59-marker panel . 28 of these were also called MSI-H by the Bethesda panel , whereas one was called MSS by the Bethesda panel .
keep_reasoning: Highlights near-complete agreement and one discordant case, useful for discussing relative sensitivity.

fact: Each of the 28 CRC tumors called MSI by the Bethesda panel was also positive with the 59-marker panel.
source_span: Each of the 28 MSI tumors on Bethesda was also positive with our 59-marker panel .
keep_reasoning: Confirms that the 59-marker panel detects all MSI cases identified by Bethesda in the CRC cohort.

fact: One colorectal tumor was MSI-positive by the 59-marker panel but not by the Bethesda panel; that tumor had a BRAF V600E mutation and MLH1 hypermethylation, indicating mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency and suggesting the 59-marker panel was more sensitive for CRC.
source_span: In contrast , one tumor was MSI-positive in the 59-marker panel but not in the Bethesda panel ( Figure 5D ) . This tumor contained a V600E BRAF mutation and was MLH1 hypermethylated , indicating that it was MMR-deficient and that our panel was also more sensitive for CRC ( Deng et al . , 2004 ) .
keep_reasoning: Provides a concrete example where the new panel detected an MMR-deficient tumor missed by the standard test, supporting improved sensitivity.

fact: The 59-marker panel correctly identified MSI in the tested ovarian tumors and leukemias in a limited sample set.
source_span: Finally , we also assessed whether our 59-marker panel can detect MSI in other cancer types . In a limited set of ovarian tumors and leukemias , we indeed correctly identified MSI in each of the samples tested ( Figure 5—source data 2 ) .
keep_reasoning: Suggests the panel's applicability beyond colorectal and endometrial cancers.

fact: The researchers observed clear signs of clonal indel selection in mismatch repair (MMR)-deficient tumors.
source_span: Since we observed clear signs of clonal indel selection in MMR-deficient tumors , we assessed whether specific pathways were enriched for indels .
keep_reasoning: This observation motivated the pathway-level analysis of indel mutations and is central to the study's mechanistic findings.

fact: The study focused on frameshift indels in exons and exon/intron boundaries because these mutations represent loss-of-function changes with less ambiguous functional impact than indels in untranslated regions (UTRs).
source_span: We focused on frameshift indels in exons and exon/intron boundaries as they represent loss-of-function mutations ( Ham et al . , 2006 ) , and thus have a less ambiguous functional impact than indels in UTRs .
keep_reasoning: Explains the rationale for focusing on a subset of indels that are most likely to disrupt gene function, which is important for lay understanding of the analysis.

fact: On average, each MMR-deficient tumor contained 472 frameshift indels in exons and exon/intron boundaries, 59 of which were recurrent indels.
source_span: On average , each MMR-deficient tumor contained 472 such indels , 59 of which were recurrent indels .
keep_reasoning: Quantifies the mutational load and recurrence in MMR-deficient tumors, which helps explain why certain pathways might be repeatedly affected.

fact: Pathway analysis using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) of all genes affected by somatic indels (excluding core MMR genes) ranked 'Role of BRCA1 in DNA damage response' as the top enriched pathway.
source_span: Pathway analyses using IPA of all genes affected by a somatic indel , excluding the core MMR genes , ranked the ‘Role of BRCA1 in DNA damage response’ as the top enriched pathway .
keep_reasoning: Points to enrichment of BRCA1-related DNA repair processes among genes mutated by indels, linking MMR deficiency to other DNA repair pathways.

fact: IPA analysis of genes affected by recurrent indels ranked the 'Double-strand break repair by homologous recombination' (DSBR by HR) pathway as the top hit.
source_span: IPA analysis of genes affected by recurrent indels moreover revealed that the ‘Double-strand break repair by homologous recombination’ pathway ( DSBR by HR ) ranked top ( Table 2 ) .
keep_reasoning: Identifies homologous recombination, a key double-strand break repair pathway, as frequently disrupted in MMR-deficient tumors.

fact: GenomeMuSiC pathway analyses using Reactome or BioCarta databases ranked the ATR/BRCA pathway and general DNA repair pathways first, with 'Homologous recombination repair' ranking third in the BioCarta-based ranking.
source_span: We also performed pathway analyses using the more advanced GenomeMuSiC , which takes background mutation rates into account and assigns weights depending on the number of tumors and genes affected in a given pathway . GenomeMuSiC analyses based on either the independently assembled Reactome or BioCarta pathway databases , ranked respectively the ‘ATR/BRCA pathway and the DNA repair’ pathway first , with the more specific ‘Homologous recombination repair’ pathway ranking third in the latter ( Table 2 ) .
keep_reasoning: Provides corroborating evidence from a different analytical method that DNA repair and homologous recombination pathways are enriched for indels.

fact: Using the curated DNARepairDB database, 'Homologous recombination' was the only DNA repair pathway significantly enriched in indels.
source_span: Based on an expert curated DNA repair database ( DNARepairDB ) , ‘Homologous recombination’ represented the only DNA repair pathway that was significantly enriched in indels .

source_span: These viruses have single-stranded , messenger-sense RNA genomes in virions .
keep_reasoning: Defines what 'positive-strand RNA virus' means, useful background for lay readers.

fact: After infection, the genomic RNAs of positive-strand RNA viruses are released into the host cell cytoplasm and translated to produce viral proteins including replication proteins.
source_span: After infection , their genomic RNAs are released into the cytoplasm of host cells and are translated to produce viral proteins including those that are required for RNA replication ( hereafter , replication proteins ) .
keep_reasoning: Explains the early steps of the viral life cycle needed to understand where host factors act.

fact: Replication proteins recruit viral genomic RNAs to intracellular membranes and synthesize complementary negative-strand RNAs.
source_span: The replication proteins recruit their genomic RNAs onto intracellular membranes and synthesize complementary , negative-strand RNAs .
keep_reasoning: Describes the role of replication proteins and the membrane localization that is central to the study.

fact: Negative-strand RNAs are sequestered with replication proteins in membrane compartments isolated from the cytosol and serve as templates to synthesize positive-strand RNAs.
source_span: The negative-strand RNAs are sequestered with the replication proteins in membranous compartments that are isolated from the cytosol , and are used as templates to synthesize positive-strand RNA ( genomic and , for certain viruses , subgenomic RNAs ) , which are released into the cytosol [1] .
keep_reasoning: Explains why membrane-bound sequestration is important for controlled replication and template use.

fact: Membrane-bound complexes that synthesize viral positive-strand RNAs are called 'replication complexes'.
source_span: The membrane-bound complexes that synthesize viral positive-strand RNAs are called ‘replication complexes’ .
keep_reasoning: Defines a key term used throughout the paper.

fact: The multiplication of positive-strand RNA viruses depends on both viral replication proteins and host factors.
source_span: The multiplication of positive-strand RNA viruses depends not only on viral replication proteins but also on host factors .
keep_reasoning: States the general concept that host cell proteins contribute to viral replication, motivating the study.

fact: Molecular chaperones such as HSP70, HSP40, HSP90, and cyclophilin B are required for efficient replication of viruses like BMV, Flock house virus, TBSV, and Hepatitis C virus, probably by modifying the structure of viral replication proteins.
source_span: For example , molecular chaperones , heat shock protein 70 ( HSP70 ) , HSP40 , HSP90 , and cyclophilin B , are required for efficient replication of BMV , Flock house virus , TBSV , and/or Hepatitis C virus , presumably by modifying the structure of viral replication proteins [7]–[11] .
keep_reasoning: Provides examples of host factors and their mechanistic role, useful for analogy and context.

fact: Eukaryotic translation elongation factor 1A (eEF1A) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) bind TBSV RNAs and are recruited to TBSV replication complexes to facilitate negative-strand and positive-strand RNA synthesis, respectively.
source_span: Eukaryotic translation elongation factor 1A ( eEF1A ) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase that can bind to positive-strand and negative-strand TBSV RNAs are recruited to TBSV replication complexes and facilitate negative-strand and positive-strand RNA synthesis , respectively [12] , [13] .
keep_reasoning: Gives a concrete example of how host metabolic and translational proteins can assist distinct steps of viral RNA synthesis.

fact: Reticulon homology proteins interact with the BMV 1a replication protein and help form spherular and double-membrane replication compartments by regulating membrane curvature.
source_span: The reticulon homology proteins interact with BMV 1a replication protein and play important roles in the formation of both spherular and double-membrane replication compartments by regulating membrane curvature [14] .
keep_reasoning: Illustrates that host membrane-shaping proteins contribute to building virus replication sites.

fact: Endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) proteins participate in forming TBSV replication compartments but are not present in mature TBSV replication complexes.
source_span: The endosomal sorting complexes required for transport ( ESCRT ) proteins also participate in the formation of TBSV replication compartments , but , unlike reticulon homology proteins , they are not present in the mature TBSV replication complexes [15] .
keep_reasoning: Shows that some host factors act transiently during replication-compartment formation rather than being permanent components.

fact: The lipid composition of cellular membranes is important for RNA replication of positive-strand RNA viruses.
source_span: Lipid composition of the membranes is also important for RNA replication of positive-strand RNA viruses [16]–[19] .
keep_reasoning: Highlights that membrane chemistry, not just proteins, affects viral replication—relevant to mechanisms discussed in the paper.

fact: Poliovirus and Coxsackievirus B3 3A proteins bind GBF1, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for ARF1, and modulate GBF1–ARF1 to recruit phosphatidylinositol-4-kinase IIIβ and facilitate formation of PI4P-enriched organelles that are essential binding sites for the viral 3D polymerase.
source_span: The 3A proteins of Poliovirus and Coxsackievirus B3 ( CVB3: a picornavirus ) bind to GBF1 , a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for a small GTP-binding protein ARF1 , and modulates the function of GBF1-ARF1 to preferentially recruit phosphatidylinositol-4-kinase IIIβ over other effectors of ARF1 and to facilitate the formation of phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate ( PI4P ) lipid-enriched organelles , which are the essential binding site for 3D polymerase [20] .
keep_reasoning: Provides a mechanistic example of how viruses can hijack host membrane and lipid machinery to build replication platforms.

fact: The Tobamovirus genus includes Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV), Youcai mosaic virus (TMV-Cg), and other related viruses.
source_span: The genus Tobamovirus includes TMV , Tomato mosaic virus ( ToMV ) , Youcai mosaic virus ( this virus is identical to TMV-Cg and , in this report , is referred to as TMV-Cg for consistency with our previous publications ) , and other related viruses .
keep_reasoning: Clarifies which viruses are in the same family as ToMV, useful for readers to relate findings across viruses.

fact: A tobamovirus genome is a non-segmented, single-stranded, 5′-capped RNA of about 6.4 kilobases that encodes a ~130 kDa replication protein, its ~180 kDa read-through product, a cell-to-cell movement protein, and a coat protein.
source_span: The genome of a tobamovirus is a non-segmented , single-stranded , 5′-capped RNA of 6 . 4 kilobases that encodes a replication protein of approximately 130 kDa ( 130K protein ) and its read-through product of 180 kDa ( 180K protein ) , a cell-to-cell movement protein , and a coat protein ( CP ) .
keep_reasoning: Gives basic genomic organization of tobamoviruses, important for explaining viral protein functions discussed in the study.

fact: The ToMV 130K protein contains a methyltransferase-like domain involved in 5′ capping of progeny RNAs and a helicase-like domain.
source_span: The 130K protein has a methyltransferase-like domain that is involved in 5′ capping of progeny RNAs and a helicase-like domain , and the read-through region of the 180K protein contains a polymerase-like domain [24] .
keep_reasoning: Specifies enzymatic domains of 130K relevant to RNA synthesis and capping discussed in the experiments.

fact: The read-through region of the ToMV 180K protein contains a polymerase-like domain.
source_span: The 130K protein has a methyltransferase-like domain that is involved in 5′ capping of progeny RNAs and a helicase-like domain , and the read-through region of the 180K protein contains a polymerase-like domain [24] .
keep_reasoning: Explains which part of the viral protein provides polymerase activity, linking protein composition to function.

fact: The 130K and 180K tobamovirus proteins are multifunctional and participate in RNA replication and RNA silencing suppression.
source_span: The 130K and 180K proteins are multifunctional proteins that participate in RNA replication and RNA silencing suppression [25] .
keep_reasoning: Summarizes key roles of the viral replication proteins that relate to how host factors might influence them.

fact: A fraction of the 130K and 180K proteins co-translationally bind the genomic RNA to form a ribonucleoprotein complex called the pre-membrane-targeting complex (PMTC), which is targeted to membrane surfaces to form viral replication complexes.
source_span: A fraction of the 130K and 180K proteins co-translationally bind to the genomic RNA to form a ribonucleoprotein complex , termed pre-membrane-targeting complex ( PMTC ) , which is targeted to membrane surfaces to form viral replication complexes .
keep_reasoning: Describes how viral proteins and RNA are directed to membranes to initiate replication, giving mechanistic context.

fact: Negative-strand RNA synthesis occurs only after the PMTC binds to membranes and the negative-strand RNAs are kept sequestered in the replication complex.
source_span: The negative-strand RNA is synthesized only after PMTC binds to membranes and kept sequestered in the replication complex [26] , [27] .
keep_reasoning: Explains the order of events and why membrane association is critical for negative-strand synthesis.

fact: A portion of the 130K protein that remains in the cytosol (non-membrane-bound) participates in RNA silencing suppression by binding double-stranded small RNAs.
source_span: Another fraction of the 130K protein that stays in the cytosol ( in a non-membrane-bound form ) participates in RNA silencing suppression by binding to double-stranded small RNAs [28] , [29] .
keep_reasoning: Clarifies the multifunctional nature and compartment-specific roles of 130K relevant to viral survival.

fact: If negative-strand RNA is synthesized in or leaks into the cytosol, it could form double-stranded RNA that would trigger RNA silencing against the viral genome.
source_span: If negative-strand RNA is synthesized in or leaks into the cytosol , it could be a source of double-stranded RNA that would trigger RNA silencing against the viral genome [15] , [30] .
keep_reasoning: Explains a cellular antiviral consequence that motivates strict sequestration of replication intermediates.

fact: Functional specialization of tobamovirus replication proteins into membrane-bound and cytosolic forms is important for successful virus multiplication and must be strictly regulated by currently undefined mechanisms.
source_span: Thus , functional specialization of the replication proteins into two alternative forms is important for the virus to multiply successfully , and should be strictly regulated by as yet undefined mechanisms .
keep_reasoning: Summarizes a conceptual point about viral strategy and remaining gaps that the study addresses.

fact: Host factors suggested to participate in tobamovirus multiplication include eEF1A, a subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3, TOM1, and TOM2A.
source_span: In tobamovirus multiplication , several host factors including eEF1A , a subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 , TOM1 , and TOM2A have been suggested to participate [31]–[35] .
keep_reasoning: Lists known host proteins implicated in tobamovirus replication, situating the current study among prior work.

fact: TOM1 and TOM2A encode seven-pass and four-pass transmembrane proteins, respectively.
source_span: TOM1 and TOM2A encode seven-pass and four-pass transmembrane proteins , respectively .
keep_reasoning: Provides structural information about host factors that relates to their membrane-associated function.

fact: In Arabidopsis, simultaneous inactivation of TOM1 and its paralog TOM3 completely inhibits multiplication of TMV-Cg and ToMV.
source_span: In A . thaliana , simultaneous inactivation of TOM1 and its paralog TOM3 results in complete inhibition of multiplication of both TMV-Cg and ToMV [36] , [37] ,
keep_reasoning: Gives genetic evidence that TOM1 (and TOM3) are essential host factors for tobamovirus infection.

fact: Knockout of TOM2A and its related genes results in incomplete inhibition of TMV-Cg multiplication and has little effect on ToMV multiplication.
source_span: whereas knockout of TOM2A and its related genes results in incomplete inhibition of TMV-Cg multiplication but had little effect on ToMV multiplication [38] .
keep_reasoning: Distinguishes the relative importance of different host membrane proteins for different tobamoviruses.

fact: Several host factors including eEF1A, a subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3, TOM1, and TOM2A have been suggested to participate in tobamovirus multiplication.
source_span: In tobamovirus multiplication, several host factors including eEF1A, a subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3, TOM1, and TOM2A have been suggested to participate [31]–[35].
keep_reasoning: Identifies host proteins implicated in virus replication, a key background point for understanding host-virus interactions studied here.

fact: In Arabidopsis thaliana, simultaneous inactivation of TOM1 and its paralog TOM3 results in complete inhibition of multiplication of both TMV-Cg and ToMV.
source_span: In A. thaliana, simultaneous inactivation of TOM1 and its paralog TOM3 results in complete inhibition of multiplication of both TMV-Cg and ToMV [36], [37].
keep_reasoning: Shows genetic evidence that TOM1 (with TOM3) is essential for tobamovirus multiplication in a model plant, motivating study of TOM1 function.

fact: Knockout of TOM2A and its related genes results in incomplete inhibition of TMV-Cg multiplication but has little effect on ToMV multiplication.
source_span: whereas knockout of TOM2A and its related genes results in incomplete inhibition of TMV-Cg multiplication but had little effect on ToMV multiplication [38].
keep_reasoning: Clarifies that TOM2A's role in virus multiplication differs between related tobamoviruses, highlighting functional differences among host factors.

fact: TOM1 interacts with tobamoviral helicase domain polypeptides and TOM2A and is thought to help tether tobamovirus replication proteins on membranes.
source_span: TOM1 interacts with tobamoviral helicase domain polypeptides and TOM2A [33], [34], [37], and is thought to help tether tobamovirus replication proteins on membranes.
keep_reasoning: Provides a mechanistic hypothesis for how TOM1 promotes viral RNA replication by anchoring viral proteins to membranes.

fact: The authors developed experimental systems to enable biochemical analyses of tobamovirus RNA replication, including a translation and replication system in evacuolated plant cell extract (BYL) and a method to prepare and purify active tobamovirus RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp).
source_span: These include a translation and replication system for tobamovirus RNA in evacuolated plant cell extract (BYL) [39] and a method to prepare and purify active tobamovirus RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) [27].
keep_reasoning: Explains the experimental toolkit that made the biochemical study of viral replication and host factors possible.

fact: A previous purified ToMV RdRp preparation contained viral replication proteins, TOM1, TOM2A, HSP70, eEF1A, and an unidentified protein of approximately 20 kDa.
source_span: Our previous study showed that the purified ToMV RdRp preparation contained viral replication proteins, TOM1, TOM2A, HSP70, eEF1A, and an unidentified protein of approximately 20 kDa [27].
keep_reasoning: Reports the composition of an RdRp preparation that led to searching for the unknown 20-kDa host component.

fact: The approximately 20-kDa unidentified protein in the RdRp preparation was identified by LC-MS/MS as a small GTP-binding protein, NtARL8.
source_span: We analyzed the 20-kDa protein using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and found that it was a small GTP-binding protein, NtARL8.
keep_reasoning: Identifies the unknown host factor, a central discovery of the study linking ARL8 to viral replication complexes.

fact: NtARL8 co-purified with the 180K-FS protein from solubilized membranes but not from the 15,000 x g supernatant of extracts of ToMV-180FS-GFP-infected and evacuolated protoplasts.
source_span: NtARL8 co-purified with the 180K-FS protein from the solubilized membranes but not from the 15,000 x g supernatant of the extract of ToMV-180FS-GFP-infected and evacuolated protoplasts (Figure 1B, lower panel).
keep_reasoning: Shows NtARL8 is specifically associated with membrane-bound viral replication protein complexes rather than soluble fractions.

fact: Four ARL8-related genes were identified from Nicotiana tabacum cv. Samsun, and proteins from at least three genes (NtARL8a, NtARL8b, NtARL8c) co-purified with ToMV 180K-FS.
source_span: By the degenerate PCR and RACE methods, we identified four ARL8-related genes from N. tabacum cv. Samsun and found by re-analyzing the LC-MS/MS data that the proteins from at least three of these genes, NtARL8a, NtARL8b, and NtARL8c, were co-purified with ToMV 180K-FS (Figure 1C; Genbank Accession Nos. AB644217-AB644220).
keep_reasoning: Establishes that multiple ARL8 paralogs in tobacco associate with the viral polymerase, supporting a conserved host role.

fact: ARL8 belongs to the ARF family of small GTP-binding proteins that include ARF and SAR proteins.
source_span: ARL8 belongs to the ARF family of small GTP-binding proteins that include ARF and SAR proteins.
keep_reasoning: Places ARL8 in a well-known protein family, useful background for explaining its likely biochemical behavior.

fact: ARF family proteins have an N-terminal amphipathic helix that participates in tight binding of the protein to membranes.
source_span: ARF family proteins have an N-terminal amphipathic helix that participates in tight binding of the protein to membranes.
keep_reasoning: Explains how ARL8-family proteins are predisposed to associate with cellular membranes, relevant to membrane-associated viral replication.

fact: ARL8 family genes are conserved in plants and animals but are not present in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source_span: ARL8 family genes are conserved in plants and animals but not in yeast S. cerevisiae (Figure 1D) [40]–[42].
keep_reasoning: Gives evolutionary context that could explain differences in host factor availability between organisms.

fact: Human, Drosophila melanogaster, and Caenorhabditis elegans ARL8 proteins mainly localize to lysosomes, and C. elegans ARL8 mediates transport of endocytosed macromolecules to lysosomes by facilitating late endosome-lysosome fusion.
source_span: Human, Drosophila melanogaster, and Caenorhabditis elegans ARL8 proteins mainly localize to lysosomes and C. elegans ARL8 mediates transport of endocytosed macromolecules to lysosomes by facilitating late endosome-lysosome fusion [43]–[45].
keep_reasoning: Describes known cellular functions and localization of ARL8 in other organisms that inform hypotheses about its role in plants and viral replication.

fact: Arabidopsis ARL8 proteins localize on vacuolar and other organellar membranes.
source_span: Arabidopsis ARL8 proteins localize on vacuolar and other organellar membranes [46].
keep_reasoning: Provides plant-specific localization information linking ARL8 to the membrane compartments relevant for tobamovirus replication.

fact: ToMV RNA replication takes place on membranes and TOM1 is also localized on vacuolar and other organellar membranes.
source_span: This is intriguing because ToMV RNA replication takes place on membranes and TOM1 is also localized on vacuolar and other organellar membranes.
keep_reasoning: Connects viral replication location with host factor localization, supporting a functional interaction hypothesis.

fact: Tobamovirus replication proteins are associated with both TOM1 and ARL8, but it was unclear whether a complex containing all three proteins is formed or whether replication proteins form distinct complexes with TOM1 and ARL8.
source_span: Tobamovirus replication proteins associated with TOM1 and ARL8 ([27] and Figure 1B); however it was unclear whether a complex containing all of the three proteins is formed or the replication proteins form distinct complexes with TOM1 and ARL8.
keep_reasoning: Frames a specific question addressed by the study about the composition of membrane-bound viral replication complexes.

fact: Affinity purification of FLAG-StrepII-tagged NtARL8a (NtARL8a-FS) from ToMV-infected BY-2 cells co-purified ToMV 130K and 180K proteins and NtTOM1.
source_span: As expected, ToMV 130K and 180K proteins were co-purified with NtARL8a-FS from infected cells (Figure 2A, bottom panel). NtTOM1 was also co-purified with NtARL8a-FS from ToMV-infected cells.
keep_reasoning: Provides experimental evidence that NtARL8, TOM1, and viral replication proteins can be part of the same membrane-associated material in infected plant cells.

fact: From uninfected cells, NtTOM1 was co-purified with NtARL8a-FS at much lower levels than from infected cells, while endogenous NtARL8 co-purified with NtARL8a-FS from both uninfected and infected cells at similar levels.
source_span: From uninfected cells, NtTOM1 was co-purified with NtARL8a-FS, but the amount was much lower than that from ToMV-infected cells (Figure 2A, fourth panel from the top). Endogenous NtARL8 was co-purified with NtARL8a-FS from uninfected and ToMV-infected cells at similar levels (Figure 2A, second panel from the top).
keep_reasoning: Shows that infection increases TOM1 association with ARL8 complexes while ARL8 self-association is constitutive, supporting infection-specific complex formation.

fact: These co-purification results suggest that a membrane-bound complex containing ToMV replication proteins, NtTOM1, and NtARL8 is formed in infected cells.
source_span: These results suggest that a membrane-bound complex that contains ToMV replication proteins, NtTOM1, and NtARL8 is formed in infected cells.
keep_reasoning: Summarizes the experimental inference that the three components assemble into a membrane-associated complex during infection.

fact: Only a small fraction of the membrane-bound replication proteins in plant cells participates in RNA synthesis.
source_span: We previously found that only a small fraction of the membrane-bound replication proteins in plant cells participates in RNA synthesis [27].
keep_reasoning: Important caveat for interpreting biochemical purifications and activity assays of replication complexes.

fact: RdRp activity assays showed similar RNA polymerase activity per 180K protein in NtARL8a-FS-purified fractions and ToMV-180FS-purified fractions despite there being less 180K protein in the NtARL8a-FS fraction, suggesting that ToMV 180K protein associated with NtARL8 is actively involved in RNA synthesis.
source_span: A larger amount of the 180K protein was found in the ToMV-180FS-purified fraction (Figure 2B, leftmost lane) than in the NtARL8a-FS-purified fraction (Figure 2B, rightmost lane), whereas a similar level of RdRp activity was detected in these two lanes. This suggests that ToMV 180K protein that associates with NtARL8 is actively involved in RNA synthesis.
keep_reasoning: Provides functional evidence linking ARL8-associated viral polymerase to active RNA synthesis, a key mechanistic conclusion.

fact: Pairwise split-ubiquitin yeast two-hybrid experiments suggested that Arabidopsis ARL8a interacts with both Arabidopsis TOM1 and a polypeptide corresponding to the helicase domain of ToMV replication proteins (amino acid residues 648-1116 of ToMV 130K).
source_span: The results suggested that AtARL8a interacts with both AtTOM1 and a polypeptide corresponding to the helicase domain of ToMV replication proteins (amino acid residues 648-1116 of ToMV 130K protein, Figure 3A, 3B).
keep_reasoning: Identifies direct or near-direct protein-protein interactions that could explain assembly of replication complexes on membranes.

fact: The ToMV helicase domain polypeptide appeared to interact with AtTOM1 in the yeast two-hybrid assay.
source_span: Consistent with our previous results using the Sos recruitment system [34], [37], the ToMV helicase domain polypeptide appeared to interact with AtTOM1 (Figure 3A).
keep_reasoning: Supports prior evidence that TOM1 binds the viral helicase domain, reinforcing the proposed tethering role of TOM1.

fact: The signals for ARL8 interactions with TOM1 and the ToMV helicase domain were 6 and 13 times weaker than the TOM1-helicase domain interaction signal in the split-ubiquitin assay.
source_span: The signals for ARL8 interactions with TOM1 and ToMV helicase domain were 6 and 13 times weaker than the TOM1-helicase domain interaction signal.
keep_reasoning: Quantifies relative interaction strengths suggesting ARL8 interactions are weaker than the direct TOM1-helicase association, which is informative for mechanistic models.

fact: AtARL8a interacts with both AtTOM1 and a polypeptide corresponding to the helicase domain of ToMV replication proteins (amino acid residues 648-1116 of ToMV 130K protein).
source_span: The results suggested that AtARL8a interacts with both AtTOM1 and a polypeptide corresponding to the helicase domain of ToMV replication proteins ( amino acid residues 648-1116 of ToMV 130K protein , Figure 3A , 3B ) .
keep_reasoning: This protein–protein interaction links a host small GTPase (ARL8) to a viral replication protein and is central to the study's mechanism.

fact: The ToMV helicase domain polypeptide appeared to interact with AtTOM1.
source_span: Consistent with our previous results using the Sos recruitment system [34] , [37] , the ToMV helicase domain polypeptide appeared to interact with AtTOM1 ( Figure 3A ) .
keep_reasoning: Demonstrates a specific interaction between a viral helicase domain and the host membrane protein TOM1, central to viral replication complex formation.

fact: Signals for ARL8 interactions with TOM1 and the ToMV helicase domain were 6- and 13-fold weaker, respectively, than the TOM1–helicase domain interaction signal.
source_span: The signals for ARL8 interactions with TOM1 and ToMV helicase domain were 6 and 13 times weaker than the TOM1-helicase domain interaction signal .
keep_reasoning: Quantifies relative strengths of interactions, suggesting a stronger TOM1–helicase direct interaction than ARL8-mediated interactions.

fact: No interaction was detected between TOM1 or ARL8 and other regions of tobamovirus replication proteins using the split-ubiquitin or Sos recruitment systems.
source_span: We could not detect an interaction between TOM1 or ARL8 and the other regions of tobamovirus replication proteins by the split-ubiquitin or Sos recruitment systems ( data not shown ) .
keep_reasoning: Defines the specificity of TOM1 and ARL8 interactions to the viral helicase domain, which helps explain interaction mapping.

fact: The ToMV 180K protein has RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) activity.
source_span: Because ToMV 180K protein , which shows RdRp activity , preferentially associates with NtARL8 ( Figure 2B ) , ARL8 may positively regulate tobamovirus multiplication .
keep_reasoning: Identifies the viral protein responsible for RNA replication, a key concept for lay readers to understand viral multiplication.

fact: ToMV 180K protein preferentially associates with NtARL8.
source_span: Because ToMV 180K protein , which shows RdRp activity , preferentially associates with NtARL8 ( Figure 2B ) , ARL8 may positively regulate tobamovirus multiplication .
keep_reasoning: Links the viral polymerase to a host ARL8 protein, supporting the idea that ARL8 helps viral replication.

fact: The Arabidopsis thaliana genome encodes four ARL8-related genes, designated AtARL8a, AtARL8b, AtARL8c, and AtARL8d.
source_span: The A . thaliana genome encodes four ARL8-related genes , designated AtARL8a-d [41] , [42] , [48] ( Figure 1C and 1D ) .
keep_reasoning: Provides necessary genetic context for the mutant analysis and gene family redundancy discussed in the study.

fact: Quantitative RT-PCR showed that AtARL8a, AtARL8c, and AtARL8d mRNA levels are about 89%, 3%, and 0.5%, respectively, of the AtARL8b mRNA level in Arabidopsis.
source_span: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis showed that mRNA levels of AtARL8a ( At3g49870 ) , AtARL8c ( At5g37680 ) , and AtARL8d ( At3g49860 ) are about 89% , 3% , and 0 . 5% , respectively , of that of AtARL8b ( At5g67560 ) .
keep_reasoning: Relative expression levels explain which family members are most abundant and likely functionally important.

fact: AtARL8d may be a pseudogene because it lacks an N-terminal part conserved among the other ARL8 proteins.
source_span: AtARL8d may be a pseudogene because it lacks an N-terminal part that is conserved among the other ARL8 proteins .
keep_reasoning: Explains why AtARL8d is unlikely to contribute to ARL8 function, relevant to interpreting mutant phenotypes.

fact: Researchers obtained Arabidopsis T-DNA or transposon insertion mutants arl8a-1, arl8b-1, and arl8c-1 and constructed all possible double and triple mutants.
source_span: We obtained A . thaliana T-DNA or transposon insertion mutants arl8a-1 , arl8b-1 , and arl8c-1 , and constructed all possible double and triple mutants .
keep_reasoning: Describes the genetic tools used to test ARL8 family function in plants.

fact: None of the arl8 single, double, or triple mutants had any apparent effect on plant growth or morphology.
source_span: None of these arl8 mutations had any apparent effect on plant growth or morphology ( Figure 4A ) .
keep_reasoning: Indicates that loss of ARL8 genes does not grossly affect plant development, focusing attention on virus-specific effects.

fact: A faint band at the position of AtARL8b protein was detected by immunoblot in the arl8b-1 single, arl8a-1 arl8b-1 double, and arl8a-1 arl8b-1 arl8c-1 triple mutants.
source_span: For the arl8b-1 single , arl8a-1 arl8b-1 double or arl8a-1 arl8b-1 arl8c-1 triple mutants , a faint band was detected at the position of the AtARL8b protein on the immunoblot ( Figure 4B , top panel ) .
keep_reasoning: Suggests residual ARL8b protein in some mutants, which is important for interpreting partial phenotypes.

fact: The arl8b-1 mutant contains a transposon fragment in an intron, which might allow a small amount of wild-type ARL8b mRNA to be produced by correct splicing.
source_span: Because a transposon fragment is inserted in one of introns in the arl8b-1 mutant , a small amount of wild-type ARL8b mRNA might be produced via splicing that correctly links the exons .
keep_reasoning: Explains the likely molecular basis for the faint ARL8b signal in arl8b-1 mutants.

fact: After inoculation with TMV-Cg and ToMV, coat proteins (CPs) were not detected in inoculated leaves of arl8a-1 arl8b-1 double or arl8a-1 arl8b-1 arl8c-1 triple mutants, whereas other arl8 mutants accumulated CP to wild-type levels.
source_span: The CPs were not detected in the inoculated leaves of arl8a-1 arl8b-1 double or arl8a-1 arl8b-1 arl8c-1 triple mutants ( Figure 4B ) , whereas in the other mutants , the CPs accumulated to a level similar to that in wild-type plants .
keep_reasoning: Shows that combined loss of ARL8 family members blocks tobamovirus accumulation in whole plants.

fact: No single mutation in ARL8 family members produced a detectable effect on tobamovirus multiplication.
source_span: That no single mutation in the ARL8 family members showed any detectable phenotype on tobamovirus multiplication may explain why we previously failed to identify arl8 alleles by screening randomly mutagenized A . thaliana plants .
keep_reasoning: Indicates functional redundancy among ARL8 genes that masks single-gene loss effects.

fact: Coat protein of Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) accumulated to wild-type levels in all arl8 mutants.
source_span: The CP of Cucumber mosaic virus ( CMV ) accumulated to wild-type levels in all of these arl8 mutants ( Figure 4B , bottom panel ) .
keep_reasoning: Shows that ARL8 loss specifically affects tobamoviruses and not all plant viruses, indicating specificity.

fact: ARL8 plays a specific and essential role in tobamovirus multiplication in planta.
source_span: These results indicate that ARL8 plays a specific and essential role in tobamovirus multiplication in planta .
keep_reasoning: States the study's main biological conclusion linking ARL8 to virus multiplication in plants.
